q: In catabolic pathways, the coenzyme NAD<sup>+</sup> functions as
c: an oxidizing agent that accepts hydrogen and is reduced to NADH
a reducing agent that donates hydrogen to the substrates
an energy store that releases a phosphate group to ADP
a carrier that transfers acetyl groups into the citric acid cycle
h: In catabolism, fuels are oxidized. What must happen to the coenzyme that removes their hydrogen?
w: NAD+ accepts two electrons and an H+ from the oxidized substrate, so it is reduced to NADH, which makes it the oxidizing agent. Coenzyme A, not NAD+, carries acetyl groups.
x: A reducing agent donates hydrogen. In catabolism the fuel is being oxidized, so the coenzyme has to take hydrogen away from it, not give hydrogen to it.
That describes ATP, which transfers a phosphate group. NAD<sup>+</sup> is an electron and hydrogen carrier, not a phosphate donor.
That is the job of coenzyme A, which carries acetyl groups as acetyl CoA. NAD<sup>+</sup> carries hydrogen and electrons instead.

q: The digestion of which type of food begins in the mouth?
h: Saliva contains an enzyme. Which macromolecule does it attack?
w: Salivary amylase starts hydrolyzing the α-glycosidic bonds of starch in the mouth. Protein digestion starts in the stomach (pepsin); fat digestion mainly occurs in the small intestine with lipase and bile salts.
x: Protein digestion starts in the stomach, where HCl and pepsin act. Think about which enzyme is in saliva.
Fat digestion happens mainly in the small intestine, with bile salts and pancreatic lipase. Saliva's enzyme works on a different nutrient.
Nucleic acids are hydrolyzed by nucleases from the pancreas in the small intestine. Saliva's enzyme attacks a different polymer.

q: What is the net number of ATP produced directly in glycolysis from one glucose molecule?
h: Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but uses some in its first (energy-investment) steps.
w: 4 ATP are formed, but 2 ATP are invested at the start, so the net yield is 2 ATP (plus 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate). 32 is the total for complete oxidation.
x: 4 is the gross number of ATP made in the payoff steps. Remember that ATP was spent in the first steps of glycolysis.
That is roughly the total for complete oxidation of glucose, including the citric acid cycle and electron transport. The question asks about glycolysis alone.
36 is an older total for complete oxidation of glucose, not the yield of glycolysis alone. Glycolysis by itself makes far less ATP.

q: During strenuous exercise, when oxygen is limited, muscle cells convert pyruvate to
h: Under anaerobic conditions, the cell must regenerate NAD<sup>+</sup> without oxygen.
w: Reducing pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue. Ethanol + CO2 is the yeast pathway; acetyl CoA forms when oxygen is plentiful.
x: Acetyl CoA forms when oxygen is plentiful, because its NADH must be reoxidized by the electron transport chain. Without enough O<sub>2</sub>, the cell needs another route.
Ethanol and CO<sub>2</sub> are made by yeast during alcoholic fermentation. Human muscle uses a different anaerobic product.
Making glucose from pyruvate (gluconeogenesis) uses energy and occurs mainly in the liver, not in a working muscle short of oxygen.

q: In transamination, the amino group of an amino acid trades places with the C=O of an α-keto acid. Alanine, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)–COOH, reacts with α-ketoglutarate, HOOC–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–CO–COOH. What are the products?
h: Alanine loses its –NH<sub>2</sub> and gets a C=O in its place; α-ketoglutarate gains the –NH<sub>2</sub>. Which 3-carbon keto acid has the formula CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–COOH?
w: Alanine's –NH2 goes to α-ketoglutarate, which becomes glutamate; alanine becomes the α-keto acid pyruvate. Free NH+4 is released later, when glutamate is oxidatively deaminated, and is converted to urea in the urea cycle.
x: Lactate would require a reduction, and glutamine forms from glutamate plus NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, not by transamination. Here the amino group simply swaps places with the C=O.
In transamination the amino group is handed to the keto acid rather than released as free ammonium. Ask which compound receives alanine's –NH<sub>2</sub>.
Oxaloacetate and aspartate form when the amino acid partner is aspartate. The reactants here are alanine and α-ketoglutarate, so look at what each one becomes.

q: Cyanide is deadly because it blocks cytochrome c oxidase, the last enzyme complex of the electron transport chain. What does this block directly?
c: the transfer of electrons to O<sub>2</sub>, stopping ATP synthesis
the breakdown of glucose to pyruvate in glycolysis
the digestion of proteins by pepsin in the stomach
the release of fatty acids from adipose (fat) cells
h: Cytochrome c oxidase is the final complex. What is the final electron acceptor?
w: Cytochrome c oxidase passes electrons to O2, forming water. With it blocked, electron flow and proton pumping stop, so oxidative phosphorylation stops making ATP. Glycolysis can still run.
x: Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol and does not use the electron transport chain, so it keeps running. Think about the last step of the chain.
Pepsin works in the stomach and has nothing to do with the electron transport chain in mitochondria.
Releasing fatty acids from adipose tissue is a hormone-controlled hydrolysis, not part of the electron transport chain. Think about what the final complex hands its electrons to.

q: One turn of the citric acid cycle produces the reduced coenzymes and GTP listed in the table. Using the ATP values given, how many ATP are produced from one acetyl CoA?
h: Multiply each coenzyme by its ATP yield, then add the GTP.
w: 3(2.5) + 1(1.5) + 1 = 7.5 + 1.5 + 1 = 10 ATP. Forgetting the GTP gives 9; forgetting the FADH2 gives 8.5; counting only the NADH gives 7.5.
x: 7.5 counts only the 3 NADH. Add in the FADH<sub>2</sub> and the GTP from one turn too.
9 leaves out the GTP made directly in the cycle. Each GTP counts as 1 ATP.
8.5 forgets the FADH<sub>2</sub>. One turn also makes 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>, worth 1.5 ATP.

q: How many acetyl CoA molecules are produced by the complete β-oxidation of stearic acid, an 18-carbon fatty acid?
h: Each acetyl CoA contains two carbons from the fatty acid chain.
w: 18 C ÷ 2 C per acetyl CoA = 9 acetyl CoA. This takes 8 cycles of β-oxidation, because the last cycle produces two acetyl CoA; answering 8 mixes up cycles and products.
x: 8 is the number of β-oxidation cycles, not the number of acetyl CoA. The last cycle releases two acetyl CoA at once.
That counts one acetyl CoA per carbon. Each acetyl CoA carries two carbons from the chain.
6 does not match the chain length. Divide the number of carbons by the carbons in each acetyl group.

q: In uncontrolled diabetes or long fasting, the liver converts excess acetyl CoA into ketone bodies. Which group lists the ketone bodies?
h: When oxaloacetate is low, acetyl CoA from fat cannot enter the citric acid cycle. What do two acetyl CoA form?
w: Ketogenesis produces acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate and acetone. Too much of these lowers blood pH (ketoacidosis), and acetone gives the fruity breath odor.
x: Pyruvate and lactate come from glycolysis, not from ketogenesis. Only acetone in this list is a ketone body.
These are the starting material and citric acid cycle compounds. Ketone bodies form when acetyl CoA cannot enter the cycle.
Glucose and glycogen are carbohydrates. Ketone bodies are made from acetyl CoA when the body is burning fat.

q: Between meals, glucagon signals the liver to break glycogen down into glucose to keep blood sugar normal. This process is called
h: Split the word: glycogen + lysis (splitting). Which name means breaking glycogen apart?
w: Breaking glycogen into glucose (via glucose-1-phosphate) is glycogenolysis. Glycogenesis is the reverse (making glycogen after a meal, stimulated by insulin), and gluconeogenesis makes new glucose from noncarbohydrate sources.
x: Glycogenesis means making glycogen from glucose, the storage process stimulated by insulin after a meal. The question describes the opposite.
Gluconeogenesis makes new glucose from noncarbohydrate sources such as lactate or amino acids. Here glucose comes from stored glycogen.
Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate. The question is about releasing glucose from a stored polymer.

q: Glycogen breakdown releases glucose-6-phosphate, which cannot leave the cell until the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase removes its phosphate. Liver and muscle both store glycogen, but only the liver releases free glucose into the blood. What is the best explanation?
c: Liver has glucose-6-phosphatase to remove the phosphate; muscle does not
Only liver has glycogen phosphorylase to split the glycogen
Muscle glycogen is a polymer of fructose instead of glucose
Muscle cells lack hexokinase, so glucose cannot be trapped
h: Glucose-6-phosphate cannot cross the cell membrane. Which enzyme turns it into free glucose?
w: Glycogenolysis gives glucose-6-phosphate, which is trapped inside the cell. The liver has glucose-6-phosphatase to remove the phosphate; muscle does not, so muscle keeps its glucose-6-phosphate for its own glycolysis. Muscle does have glycogen phosphorylase.
x: Muscle does have glycogen phosphorylase and breaks down its own glycogen. The difference lies in what happens to glucose-6-phosphate afterward.
Muscle glycogen, like liver glycogen, is a polymer of glucose. Both tissues store the same polymer.
Muscle cells do have hexokinase. The issue is removing the phosphate so glucose can leave the cell, not adding it.

q: Gluconeogenesis builds glucose from pyruvate or from glycolysis intermediates, but the step pyruvate → acetyl CoA cannot be reversed. Which compound CANNOT be used by the liver to make a net amount of new glucose?
h: Gluconeogenesis starts from pyruvate or a glycolysis intermediate. Which molecule is formed only after pyruvate has irreversibly lost a CO<sub>2</sub>?
w: Lactate and alanine (→ pyruvate) and glycerol (→ dihydroxyacetone phosphate) can all become glucose. Pyruvate → acetyl CoA is irreversible, and the 2 carbons of acetyl CoA leave as 2 CO2 in the citric acid cycle, so acetyl CoA from fatty acids gives no net glucose.
x: Lactate is oxidized back to pyruvate, which gluconeogenesis can turn into glucose (the Cori cycle). Look for a molecule formed after pyruvate's irreversible step.
Glycerol is converted to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, a glycolysis intermediate, so it can be made into glucose.
Alanine is transaminated to pyruvate, which can be made into glucose. It is a glucogenic amino acid.

q: In the Cori cycle, lactate produced by hard-working muscle travels in the blood to the liver, where it is
c: converted back to glucose, which returns to the muscle
converted to urea, which is excreted by the kidneys
converted to triacylglycerol, which is stored in fat cells
oxidized to acetone, which is exhaled through the lungs
h: The Cori cycle recycles muscle lactate. What useful fuel can the liver rebuild from it?
w: The liver oxidizes lactate to pyruvate and uses gluconeogenesis to make glucose, which returns to the muscle through the blood. Urea comes from amino-acid nitrogen, not from lactate.
x: Urea is made from amino-acid nitrogen. Lactate contains no nitrogen, so it cannot become urea.
Storing the carbons as fat would not help the muscle keep working. The Cori cycle returns usable fuel to the muscle.
Acetone is a ketone body made from acetyl CoA during fasting or diabetes. Lactate is recycled into something more useful.

q: The pentose phosphate pathway is especially active in fat-forming cells and red blood cells. Its main products are
h: Fat synthesis needs a reducing coenzyme, and nucleotides need a five-carbon sugar. Which pair fits?
w: The pentose phosphate pathway oxidizes glucose-6-phosphate to give NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate. NADPH supplies reducing power for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis and protects red cells from oxidation; ribose is used to build nucleotides. NADH and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate belong to glycolysis.
x: NADH and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate are associated with glycolysis. Biosynthesis needs a different reducing coenzyme and a five-carbon sugar.
FADH<sub>2</sub> and acetyl CoA come from β-oxidation and pyruvate oxidation. Neither supplies the 5-carbon sugar needed for nucleotides.
ATP and lactate come from glycolysis and fermentation. This pathway's job is to supply reducing power and a pentose.

q: When bread dough rises, yeast cells growing without oxygen convert pyruvate into
h: Think fermentation. Which gas makes the dough rise, and what alcohol is in beer?
w: In alcoholic fermentation, yeast decarboxylates pyruvate to acetaldehyde and then reduces it, giving ethanol and CO2 (the gas that raises the dough). Human muscle makes lactate instead, and acetyl CoA forms only under aerobic conditions.
x: Lactate is made by human muscle under low oxygen. Yeast uses a different fermentation, and it releases a gas that raises the dough.
Acetyl CoA forms only when oxygen is available. The question says the yeast is growing without oxygen.
Pyruvate cannot be turned into glucose and O<sub>2</sub> by yeast. Fermentation does not produce oxygen.

q: Under aerobic conditions, pyruvate enters the mitochondria and is converted to acetyl CoA. Besides acetyl CoA, this reaction produces
h: Pyruvate has 3 carbons and an acetyl group has 2. Where does the extra carbon go, and which coenzyme is reduced?
w: Pyruvate + NAD+ + CoA → acetyl CoA + CO2 + NADH. The 3-carbon pyruvate loses one carbon as CO2 and is oxidized while NAD+ is reduced to NADH. O2 is consumed only later, in the electron transport chain.
x: O<sub>2</sub> is not produced here; it is consumed only later, in the electron transport chain. Ask where pyruvate's third carbon goes.
The carbon count is right, but FAD is not the coenzyme reduced in this step. FAD is used when a C=C forms, as in succinate → fumarate.
Water and ATP are not direct products of this step. The 3-carbon pyruvate loses one carbon as a gas and a coenzyme is reduced.

q: Why do muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactate when oxygen is in short supply?
c: to regenerate NAD<sup>+</sup> so glycolysis can continue
to make extra ATP in the lactate-forming step
to make CO<sub>2</sub> for use in the citric acid cycle
to store glucose carbons as lactate for later
h: Glycolysis uses up NAD<sup>+</sup>. Without O<sub>2</sub>, NADH cannot be reoxidized by the electron transport chain. What does pyruvate → lactate do to NADH?
w: Pyruvate + NADH → lactate + NAD+. This step regenerates NAD+, which glycolysis needs for its oxidation step, so the cell can keep making 2 ATP per glucose. The lactate step itself makes no ATP.
x: Pyruvate → lactate makes no ATP at all. Its purpose involves the coenzyme that glycolysis keeps using up.
Converting pyruvate to lactate releases no CO<sub>2</sub>; the carbon count stays at 3. Think about the NADH made earlier in glycolysis.
Lactate is not a storage form; storage would be glycogen. The step solves a coenzyme problem so glycolysis can keep going.

q: Where in the cell do glycolysis and the citric acid cycle take place?
c: glycolysis in the cytosol; the citric acid cycle in the mitochondrial matrix
glycolysis in the mitochondrial matrix; the citric acid cycle in the cytosol
glycolysis and the citric acid cycle both in the cytosol of the cell
glycolysis and the citric acid cycle both in the inner mitochondrial membrane
h: Glycolysis works even in red blood cells, which have no mitochondria.
w: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol; pyruvate then moves into the mitochondria, where the citric acid cycle runs in the matrix. The electron transport chain and ATP synthase are in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
x: This has the two locations reversed. Red blood cells have no mitochondria yet still carry out glycolysis.
The citric acid cycle needs pyruvate to move into an organelle first. Only one of the two pathways runs in the cytosol.
The inner mitochondrial membrane holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, not glycolysis or the citric acid cycle.

q: After a meal with more carbohydrate than the body needs, the liver makes fatty acids from acetyl CoA (lipogenesis). This pathway
c: adds 2 carbons per cycle and uses NADPH as the reducing agent
adds 2 carbons per cycle and produces NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub>
removes 2 carbons per cycle and uses NADPH as the reducing agent
adds 3 carbons per cycle and uses FAD as the oxidizing agent
h: Building a fatty acid is a reduction, the opposite of β-oxidation. Which coenzyme supplies the electrons for biosynthesis?
w: Lipogenesis builds the chain 2 carbons at a time (acetyl CoA via malonyl CoA) and uses NADPH to reduce C=O groups to CH2. Removing 2 carbons and producing NADH and FADH2 describes β-oxidation, the catabolic opposite.
x: Producing NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> is what β-oxidation does when it breaks a chain down. Building a chain needs a reducing agent instead.
Removing 2 carbons per cycle describes β-oxidation, the breakdown pathway. Lipogenesis lengthens the chain.
Fatty acids grow 2 carbons at a time, which is why most have an even number of carbons, and building them is a reduction, not an oxidation by FAD.

q: When a cell already has plenty of ATP and NADH, what happens to the rate of the citric acid cycle?
c: It slows, because ATP and NADH inhibit key enzymes of the cycle
It speeds up, because ATP activates the enzymes of the cycle
It speeds up, so the extra energy can be stored as GTP
It is unchanged, because the citric acid cycle is not regulated
h: Feedback control: if the cell already has lots of energy, should an energy-producing pathway speed up or slow down?
w: High ATP and NADH signal plenty of energy, so they inhibit key enzymes of the cycle, slowing it (feedback control). High ADP and NAD+ (low energy) speed it up.
x: ATP signals that energy is already plentiful, so it does not activate the enzymes of an energy-producing pathway.
Cells do not store extra energy as GTP. When energy is high, energy-producing pathways are turned down.
The citric acid cycle is regulated; several of its enzymes respond to the cell's energy level.

q: In the electron transport chain, the final electron acceptor is ____, which is reduced to ____.
h: Why do we need to breathe? Think about what happens to the oxygen we inhale.
w: At the end of the chain (cytochrome c oxidase), electrons combine with O2 and H+ to form H2O. NAD+ and FAD carry electrons into the chain; they are not the final acceptor.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup>/NADH carries electrons into the chain at Complex I. The final acceptor sits at the other end.
CO<sub>2</sub> is a waste product of catabolism, and making glucose from it is photosynthesis, not electron transport.
FAD/FADH<sub>2</sub> delivers electrons into the chain. Think about why we breathe in a certain gas.

q: According to the chemiosmotic model, what directly provides the energy for ATP synthase to make ATP?
c: H<sup>+</sup> flowing back into the matrix down its gradient
electrons passing from FADH<sub>2</sub> directly onto ADP
O<sub>2</sub> binding to ATP synthase inside the matrix
hydrolysis of GTP made in the citric acid cycle
h: The electron transport chain pumps H<sup>+</sup> into the intermembrane space. What happens when those ions return?
w: Electron transport pumps H+ into the intermembrane space, building a proton gradient. H+ flowing back into the matrix through ATP synthase drives the joining of ADP and Pi. Electrons never go to ADP directly.
x: Electrons never go to ADP. They travel through the chain to O<sub>2</sub>, and the energy is stored in a different form first.
O<sub>2</sub> accepts electrons at Complex IV; it does not bind ATP synthase. Think about the ions pumped across the membrane.
GTP from the cycle is made by substrate-level phosphorylation and is not what drives ATP synthase.

q: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP), once sold as a diet pill, carries H<sup>+</sup> back across the inner mitochondrial membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. What is the result?
c: O<sub>2</sub> use continues, but energy is released as heat instead of ATP
electron transport stops, and O<sub>2</sub> use falls to zero
ATP synthesis increases because more H<sup>+</sup> enter the matrix
glycolysis stops because NAD<sup>+</sup> can no longer be regenerated
h: An uncoupler separates electron transport from ATP synthesis. Does electron flow stop, or only ATP production?
w: DNP lets the proton gradient leak away, so electron transport and O2 use continue (even speed up), but the energy is lost as heat instead of being captured as ATP, causing dangerous fever. Stopping electron transport completely is what cyanide does.
x: Stopping electron transport is what cyanide does. DNP only provides a leak for H<sup>+</sup>, so electrons still flow to O<sub>2</sub>.
The H<sup>+</sup> that leak back through DNP bypass ATP synthase, so they cannot drive ATP production. ATP synthesis falls.
Glycolysis is in the cytosol and is not directly blocked by DNP. With electron transport still running, NADH is still reoxidized.

q: Why does each FADH<sub>2</sub> produce only about 1.5 ATP, while each NADH produces about 2.5 ATP?
c: FADH<sub>2</sub> enters the chain after complex I, so fewer H<sup>+</sup> are pumped
FADH<sub>2</sub> carries only one electron, while NADH carries two
FADH<sub>2</sub> passes its electrons straight to O<sub>2</sub> at the end
FADH<sub>2</sub> is made in the cytosol and must be moved inside
h: Compare where each carrier hands its electrons to the chain and how many proton pumps the electrons pass through.
w: NADH gives its electrons to complex I, but FADH2 gives them to coenzyme Q (through complex II), skipping complex I, so fewer protons are pumped and less ATP is made. Both carriers deliver 2 electrons.
x: Both FADH<sub>2</sub> and NADH carry two electrons. The difference is where in the chain they hand those electrons over.
FADH<sub>2</sub> electrons still pass through Complexes III and IV before reaching O<sub>2</sub>. Consider which earlier pump they skip.
The FADH<sub>2</sub> of the citric acid cycle is made inside the mitochondrion, at Complex II. Location is not the reason.

q: Using the ATP values in the table, how many ATP form when one pyruvate is completely oxidized to CO<sub>2</sub> (conversion to acetyl CoA plus one turn of the citric acid cycle)?
h: Count the NADH from pyruvate → acetyl CoA, then the NADH, FADH<sub>2</sub> and GTP from one turn of the cycle.
w: Pyruvate → acetyl CoA: 1 NADH = 2.5 ATP. One turn: 3 NADH × 2.5 = 7.5, 1 FADH2 × 1.5 = 1.5, 1 GTP = 1, total 10. Sum = 2.5 + 10 = 12.5 ATP. 13.5 counts the FADH2 as 2.5; 15 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH2; 25 is for two pyruvates (one glucose).
x: 15 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use 2.5 and 1.5 from the table.
13.5 counts the FADH<sub>2</sub> as 2.5 ATP, like an NADH. FADH<sub>2</sub> is worth only 1.5.
25 is the yield for two pyruvates, one whole glucose. The question asks about one pyruvate.

q: In the small intestine, bile salts help digest dietary fat by
c: emulsifying fat into small droplets that lipase can reach
hydrolyzing ester bonds to release free fatty acids
carrying fatty acids through the blood as lipoproteins
oxidizing fatty acids to acetyl CoA for quick energy
h: Bile salts act like detergents; enzymes do the actual bond breaking. What does a detergent do to a large blob of grease?
w: Bile salts (made from cholesterol) emulsify fat into tiny droplets, greatly increasing the surface area so pancreatic lipase can hydrolyze the ester bonds. The hydrolysis itself is done by lipase, not by bile salts.
x: Hydrolyzing ester bonds is the job of the enzyme lipase. Bile salts are not enzymes; they act like detergents.
Lipoproteins such as chylomicrons carry fat in the blood and lymph. Bile salts work inside the intestine, before absorption.
Oxidizing fatty acids to acetyl CoA is β-oxidation, which happens in mitochondria of cells, not in the intestine.

q: Palmitic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>14</sub>COOH, is completely oxidized. Using the ATP values in the table, what is the net ATP yield?
h: A 16-carbon acid gives 8 acetyl CoA. The number of β-oxidation cycles is one less than that; each cycle gives 1 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>.
w: 16 C → 8 acetyl CoA from 7 cycles. 8 × 10 = 80; 7 NADH × 2.5 = 17.5; 7 FADH2 × 1.5 = 10.5; activation −2. Net = 80 + 17.5 + 10.5 − 2 = 106 ATP. 108 forgets the activation cost; 110 uses 8 cycles instead of 7; 129 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH2.
x: 108 leaves out the 2-ATP cost of activating the fatty acid. Subtract it at the end.
110 uses 8 β-oxidation cycles. A 16-carbon acid needs one fewer cycle than its number of acetyl CoA.
129 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use the values in the table.

q: Lauric acid, a 12-carbon saturated fatty acid in coconut oil, undergoes β-oxidation. How many NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> are produced by the β-oxidation cycles themselves (not counting the citric acid cycle)?
h: Each cycle cuts off 2 carbons and makes 1 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>. The last cycle splits a 4-carbon unit into two acetyl CoA.
w: 12 C gives 6 acetyl CoA, which needs 6 − 1 = 5 cycles. Each cycle yields 1 NADH and 1 FADH2, so 5 NADH and 5 FADH2. 6 and 6 is the common mistake of counting one cycle per acetyl CoA.
x: This counts one cycle per acetyl CoA. The last cycle splits a 4-carbon unit into two acetyl CoA, so there is one fewer cycle.
Each cycle makes exactly one NADH and one FADH<sub>2</sub>, so the two numbers must be equal.
Each cycle makes exactly one NADH and one FADH<sub>2</sub>, so the two numbers must be equal.

q: A patient with uncontrolled type 1 diabetes has fruity-smelling breath and a blood pH of 7.1. What best explains the low blood pH?
c: acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are acids made from extra acetyl CoA
acetone is a strong acid that is formed from the excess blood glucose
lactate builds up because the cells are receiving too much insulin
urea builds up because amino acids are broken down too quickly
h: Without insulin, cells burn fat and the liver is flooded with acetyl CoA. Which of its products are carboxylic acids?
w: With little insulin, fat breakdown makes more acetyl CoA than the citric acid cycle can use, so the liver makes ketone bodies. Acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid are acids that lower blood pH (diabetic ketoacidosis). Acetone causes the fruity breath but is a neutral ketone, not an acid.
x: Acetone causes the fruity breath, but it is a neutral ketone, not an acid, and it comes from acetyl CoA, not from glucose.
Too little insulin, not too much, is the problem in type 1 diabetes. Look at what the liver makes from extra acetyl CoA.
Urea is a neutral compound and does not explain the low pH. The fruity breath points to a different set of products.

q: Oxidative deamination of glutamate releases NH+4, which is toxic. In the liver, this NH+4 is
c: converted to urea in the urea cycle and excreted in urine
converted to uric acid and stored in the joints as crystals
oxidized to nitrate ions and exhaled through the lungs
stored in fat cells as a reserve of amino-acid nitrogen
h: Ammonium must be changed into a less toxic, water-soluble compound that the kidneys can remove.
w: The liver combines NH+4 with CO2 (and nitrogen from aspartate) in the urea cycle, forming urea, which the kidneys excrete. In liver failure, ammonia builds up in the blood. Uric acid comes from purine breakdown, not amino acids.
x: Uric acid comes from breaking down purines in nucleic acids, and its crystals cause gout. Ammonium from amino acids is handled another way.
Nitrogen from amino acids is not oxidized to nitrate or exhaled. It must be made into a water-soluble compound the kidneys can remove.
The body has no storage form for amino-acid nitrogen in fat cells. Excess NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> must be detoxified and excreted.

q: Which process is an example of anabolism?
c: oxidation of fatty acids to acetyl CoA
breakdown of proteins to amino acids
h: Anabolic pathways build larger molecules and use energy; catabolic pathways break molecules down and release energy.
w: Making glycogen from many glucose units builds a larger molecule and requires energy (UTP), so it is anabolic. The other three break molecules into smaller ones, which is catabolism.
x: Hydrolyzing starch breaks a polymer into smaller glucose units. That is catabolism (digestion).
β-Oxidation breaks fatty acids into 2-carbon pieces and releases energy, so it is catabolic.
Breaking proteins into amino acids splits a large molecule into smaller ones, which is catabolism.

q: In the citric acid cycle, malate is converted to oxaloacetate: a –CH(OH)– group becomes a C=O group. How is this step labeled?
c: oxidation; NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced to NADH
reduction; NADH is oxidized to NAD<sup>+</sup>
oxidation; FAD is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>
hydration; H<sub>2</sub>O is added to the molecule
h: Count hydrogens: are 2 H removed or added? Then match the coenzyme to the group: alcohol → C=O or –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– → –CH=CH–.
w: Converting an alcohol (–CH(OH)–) to a ketone (C=O) removes 2 H: an oxidation. Alcohol → carbonyl oxidations use NAD+, which is reduced to NADH + H+. FAD is used when C–C becomes C=C.
x: Going from –CH(OH)– to C=O removes hydrogen, so the substrate loses H, not gains it. Check whether the coenzyme gains or loses H.
Removing 2 H makes this an oxidation, but FAD is used when a C–C becomes a C=C. Here an alcohol becomes a carbonyl.
No water is added; a C=O forms from an alcohol by removing two H atoms. Hydration adds water across a C=C.

q: In the citric acid cycle, fumarate (–CH=CH–) reacts to form malate (–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(OH)–). How is this step labeled?
c: hydration; H<sub>2</sub>O adds across the C=C
oxidation; NAD<sup>+</sup> accepts two H atoms
dehydration; H<sub>2</sub>O is removed from the C–C
h: Compare formulas: what was added across the double bond, an H on one carbon and an OH on the other?
w: An H adds to one carbon and an –OH to the other, so H2O has added across the double bond: hydration. No coenzyme is needed. Dehydration is the reverse (removing water to make a C=C).
x: No hydrogen is removed, and no coenzyme is involved. Compare formulas: something is added across the double bond.
Dehydration removes water to make a C=C. Here the C=C disappears and an –OH appears, so this is the reverse process.
No carbon is lost; fumarate and malate both have 4 carbons. Look at what adds across the C=C.

q: In the citric acid cycle, isocitrate (6 C) is converted to α-ketoglutarate (5 C) as an –OH group becomes C=O, a CO<sub>2</sub> is released, and NAD<sup>+</sup> becomes NADH. How is this step best described?
h: Two things happen: the carbon count drops by one, and an alcohol becomes a ketone using NAD<sup>+</sup>.
w: Losing CO2 (6 C → 5 C) is a decarboxylation, and alcohol → ketone with NAD+ → NADH is an oxidation: oxidative decarboxylation. “Carboxylation” would add CO2, not remove it.
x: Carboxylation adds CO<sub>2</sub> and reduction adds hydrogen. Here a CO<sub>2</sub> leaves and NAD<sup>+</sup> takes away hydrogen, so both words point the wrong way.
That fits citrate → isocitrate, the step before. This step loses a carbon and reduces NAD<sup>+</sup>.
Substrate-level phosphorylation makes GTP or ATP directly, as in succinyl CoA → succinate. No phosphate transfer happens here.

q: The last step of glycolysis is shown below. Which description fits this step?
c: a phosphate is transferred to ADP, forming ATP
PEP is oxidized as NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced to NADH
a phosphate is added to pyruvate, using up an ATP
CO<sub>2</sub> is removed from PEP in a decarboxylation
h: Track the phosphate group: which molecule loses it and which gains it?
w: PEP loses its phosphate group and ADP is phosphorylated to ATP (substrate-level phosphorylation). This step makes ATP rather than using it, and no NAD+ or CO2 is involved.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> is not used in this step; no hydrogen is removed. Follow the phosphate group instead.
Pyruvate is the product, and it has no phosphate. This step makes ATP rather than spending it.
PEP and pyruvate both have 3 carbons, so no CO<sub>2</sub> is lost. Track where the phosphate group goes.

q: In the citric acid cycle, citrate is converted to isocitrate. Both have the formula C6H5O3−7; only the –OH group moves to the neighboring carbon. How is this step labeled?
h: Compare the formulas of the reactant and product. Did anything get added or removed overall?
w: Same formula, different arrangement: isomerization (it happens by removing and then re-adding water). There is no loss of H (oxidation), no water consumed overall (hydrolysis) and no CO2 lost.
x: Oxidation removes H atoms, but the formula is unchanged. Nothing has been lost overall.
Hydrolysis would split a bond using water and change the formula. Here reactant and product have the same formula.
Decarboxylation removes CO<sub>2</sub>, which would lower the carbon count. Both compounds have 6 carbons.

q: In the final step of each β-oxidation cycle, a 2-carbon acetyl unit is split off from the fatty acyl chain, and the shortened chain is attached to a new coenzyme. Which coenzyme is it?
h: The shortened fatty acid must stay “activated” as a thioester (acyl-CoA) to enter the next cycle.
w: Thiolysis uses HS–CoA to cleave the bond, releasing acetyl CoA and a fatty acyl CoA two carbons shorter. Acetyl CoA is the product that leaves, not the coenzyme that attaches; NAD+ and FAD are the oxidizing agents in earlier steps of the cycle.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> oxidizes the –OH to C=O in step 3. It does not attach to the shortened chain.
FAD forms the C=C in step 1 of each cycle. It does not become part of the shortened acyl chain.
Acetyl CoA is the 2-carbon product that leaves. The shortened chain needs a fresh coenzyme to stay activated as a thioester.

q: A granola bar contains the nutrients listed in the table. Using the energy values given, what is its energy content?
h: Multiply each mass by its energy value (4, 9, 4 kcal g⁻¹) and add.
w: (24.0 g × 4 kcal g⁻¹) + (9.0 g × 9 kcal g⁻¹) + (6.0 g × 4 kcal g⁻¹) = 96 + 81 + 24 = 201 kcal. Using 4 kcal g⁻¹ for everything gives 156 kcal; switching the fat and protein values gives 186 kcal; leaving out the protein gives 177 kcal.
x: 156 kcal uses 4 kcal g⁻¹ for every nutrient. Fat provides 9 kcal g⁻¹.
177 kcal leaves out the protein. Include all three nutrients from the table.
186 kcal switches the fat and protein values. Fat is the nutrient worth 9 kcal g⁻¹.

q: A serving of a snack food contains the nutrients listed in the table. Using the energy values given, what percent of its Calories come from fat?
h: Find the kcal from each nutrient first, then divide fat kcal by the total kcal.
w: Fat: 12.0 × 9 = 108 kcal; carbohydrate: 30.0 × 4 = 120 kcal; protein: 8.0 × 4 = 32 kcal; total = 260 kcal. 108/260 × 100 = 42%. 47% leaves the protein out of the total (108/228); 58% is the percent that does not come from fat; 71% divides the fat kcal by the carbohydrate and protein kcal only (108/152).
x: 47% leaves the protein out of the total. Divide by the kcal from all three nutrients.
71% divides the fat kcal by only the carbohydrate and protein kcal. The total must include the fat kcal too.
58% is the share of Calories that does not come from fat. Find the fat portion instead.

q: Myristic acid is a saturated fatty acid with 14 carbons. How many β-oxidation cycles are needed to break it down completely, and how many acetyl CoA are produced?
h: Each cycle removes one 2-carbon unit, but the last cycle leaves two acetyl CoA at once.
w: Acetyl CoA = 14/2 = 7. Cycles = 14/2 − 1 = 6 cycles; 7 acetyl CoA. The final cycle splits a 4-carbon chain into two acetyl CoA, so one fewer cycle than acetyl CoA is needed.
x: 7 cycles counts one cycle per acetyl CoA. The last cycle splits a 4-carbon unit into two acetyl CoA, so one fewer cycle is needed.
6 cycles is right, but the last cycle releases two acetyl CoA at once. Divide the carbons by 2 for the acetyl CoA count.
Each acetyl CoA carries 2 carbons, so 14 acetyl CoA would need 28 carbons. The cycle count is also one too many.

q: Arachidic acid is a saturated fatty acid with 20 carbons. Using the ATP values in the table (subtract the activation cost), how many ATP form from its complete oxidation?
h: Cycles = C/2 − 1, acetyl CoA = C/2, and each cycle gives 1 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>.
w: 10 acetyl CoA × 10 = 100; 9 cycles → 9 NADH × 2.5 = 22.5 and 9 FADH2 × 1.5 = 13.5. Total 136 − 2 (activation) = 134 ATP. 136 forgets the activation cost; 138 uses 10 cycles instead of 9.
x: 136 forgets to subtract the 2 ATP spent activating the fatty acid.
138 uses 10 β-oxidation cycles. The number of cycles is one less than the number of acetyl CoA.
140 uses 10 cycles and also leaves out the 2-ATP activation cost.

q: In the electron transport chain, a mitochondrion oxidizes the reduced coenzymes listed in the table. How many ATP are produced?
h: Multiply each coenzyme by its own ATP value. NADH gives more ATP than FADH<sub>2</sub>.
w: 4 NADH × 2.5 = 10 ATP and 2 FADH2 × 1.5 = 3 ATP; total = 13 ATP. Using 2.5 for both coenzymes gives 15; the older values of 3 and 2 give 16; using 3 for all six coenzymes gives 18.
x: 18 counts all six coenzymes at 3 ATP each. Use the table: NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> have different values.
15 uses 2.5 ATP for every coenzyme. FADH<sub>2</sub> gives less ATP than NADH.
16 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use 2.5 and 1.5 from the table.

q: A student eats a turkey sandwich. In her stomach and small intestine, the turkey's proteins are hydrolyzed into free amino acids. Which stage of catabolism is this?
h: Stage 1 breaks big food molecules into their building blocks; stage 2 turns those into pyruvate or acetyl CoA.
w: Hydrolyzing polymers (proteins, starch, fats) into monomers is stage 1, digestion. Stage 2 would degrade the amino acids further to smaller compounds such as acetyl CoA; stage 3 oxidizes acetyl CoA in the citric acid cycle and electron transport.
x: Stage 2 starts after the amino acids are absorbed, when they are degraded to smaller compounds such as acetyl CoA. Here the protein is just being cut into monomers.
Stage 3 is the citric acid cycle and electron transport inside mitochondria. Breaking food proteins in the gut happens much earlier.
Anabolism builds larger molecules. Hydrolyzing proteins into amino acids breaks molecules down.

q: Electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation, which make most of a cell's ATP, are part of which stage of catabolism?
h: Glycolysis and β-oxidation stop at pyruvate or acetyl CoA. Which stage finishes the job and uses O<sub>2</sub>?
w: Acetyl CoA is oxidized in the citric acid cycle, and the NADH and FADH2 it makes feed electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation: stage 3, oxidation. Stage 2 (glycolysis, β-oxidation) only produces pyruvate and acetyl CoA; stage 1 is digestion.
x: Stage 2 includes glycolysis and β-oxidation, which stop at pyruvate or acetyl CoA. Electron transport comes after that.
Stage 1 is digestion of food polymers into monomers in the gut. It produces no NADH for electron transport.
Electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation release energy from fuel, which is catabolism, not anabolism.

q: A patient has had most of his stomach surgically removed. The normal starting point for digesting which nutrient has been lost?
h: Think about which digestive enzyme works in an acidic environment and where each nutrient's digestion begins.
w: Protein digestion begins in the stomach, where HCl and pepsin start hydrolyzing peptide bonds. Starch digestion begins in the mouth (salivary amylase), and fats and lactose are digested mainly in the small intestine, so those starting sites are untouched.
x: Starch digestion begins in the mouth with salivary amylase, which the surgery does not affect.
Triacylglycerols are digested mainly in the small intestine with bile salts and pancreatic lipase.
Lactose is digested in the small intestine by lactase. Think about which digestive enzyme works in an acidic environment.

q: In the liver, lactate, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)–COO<sup>−</sup>, is converted back to pyruvate, CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–COO<sup>−</sup>. Which coenzyme change accompanies this step?
h: Compare the carbon with the –OH before and after. Did it lose H atoms (oxidation) or gain them? Which coenzyme handles C–O bonds?
w: A C–OH becomes C=O: two H atoms are removed, so lactate is oxidized. Alcohol → carbonyl oxidations use NAD+, which is reduced: NAD+ → NADH + H+. FAD is used when a C=C forms; NADH + H+ → NAD+ would be the reverse reaction (pyruvate → lactate in muscle).
x: FAD is used when a C–C single bond becomes a C=C. Here an alcohol is oxidized to a C=O.
This is the coenzyme change for pyruvate → lactate in muscle, the reverse direction. Here lactate loses two H atoms.
No phosphate is transferred in this step. Compare the C–OH carbon before and after to see whether H is removed.

q: When ketone bodies form during fasting, acetoacetate, CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>–COO<sup>−</sup>, can be turned into β-hydroxybutyrate, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)–CH<sub>2</sub>–COO<sup>−</sup>. Which statement about the coenzyme is TRUE?
c: NADH is the reducing agent and is oxidized to NAD<sup>+</sup>.
NAD<sup>+</sup> is the oxidizing agent and is reduced to NADH.
NADH is the oxidizing agent and is reduced to NAD<sup>+</sup>.
FAD is the oxidizing agent and is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>.
h: C=O becoming CH–OH means the substrate gained H. Something had to donate it. A reducing agent itself gets oxidized.
w: The ketone C=O gains two H to become an alcohol: the substrate is reduced. The H comes from NADH + H+, so NADH is the reducing agent and is oxidized to NAD+. NAD+ → NADH would be the opposite direction (alcohol → ketone).
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> → NADH would accompany an oxidation, alcohol → ketone. Here the ketone C=O gains hydrogen to become an alcohol.
The direction is right, but NADH donates hydrogen, which makes it a reducing agent. An agent that is oxidized cannot be the oxidizing agent.
FAD is used for C–C → C=C oxidations. This step adds hydrogen to a C=O, so the substrate is reduced, not oxidized.

q: Succinate dehydrogenase, the citric acid cycle enzyme that converts succinate to fumarate, is part of Complex II in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Using the electron transport chain shown, to which electron carrier does its FADH<sub>2</sub> pass electrons?
h: FADH<sub>2</sub> electrons enter the chain after Complex I. Which mobile carrier collects electrons from both Complex I and Complex II?
w: Complex II hands electrons from FADH2 to coenzyme Q (CoQ → CoQH2), which carries them to Complex III. Because they skip Complex I, fewer protons are pumped, which is why FADH2 gives only about 1.5 ATP.
x: Cytochrome c carries electrons from Complex III to Complex IV. FADH<sub>2</sub> electrons reach an earlier carrier first.
FADH<sub>2</sub> electrons skip Complex I entirely, which is why they pump fewer protons.
O<sub>2</sub> accepts electrons only at Complex IV, at the end of the chain. FADH<sub>2</sub> electrons still pass through several carriers first.

q: In the energy-investment half of glycolysis, how many ATP are used per glucose molecule?
h: Count the steps where a phosphate is added from ATP before fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is split.
w: ATP is spent twice: glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase) and fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. That is 2 ATP invested. 4 ATP are made later, which is why the net yield is 2.
x: Count again: ATP is spent at two separate phosphorylation steps before fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is split.
4 ATP are made in the energy-payoff half, not spent in the investment half.
The first half is called the investment phase because it does spend ATP. Look for the steps where a phosphate is added from ATP.

q: In the glycolysis pathway shown, NADH is produced in only one step. Which conversion is it?
h: Find the step where NAD<sup>+</sup> goes in and NADH comes out. In that step an aldehyde carbon is oxidized.
w: In the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate → 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate step, the aldehyde (–CHO) is oxidized as Pi is attached, and NAD+ is reduced to NADH. The other three steps are phosphate transfers involving ATP and need no NAD+.
x: This step adds a phosphate from ATP. No hydrogen is removed, so NAD<sup>+</sup> is not involved.
This step transfers PEP's phosphate to ADP, making ATP. It is not an oxidation.
This first step adds a phosphate from ATP to glucose. Look for the step where an aldehyde carbon is oxidized.

q: In the citric acid cycle shown, which step forms GTP (or ATP) directly, without electron transport?
h: Find GTP on the wheel. It forms at the step where the high-energy thioester of succinyl CoA is hydrolyzed.
w: Hydrolysis of the thioester in succinyl CoA → succinate is downhill enough overall (breaking the bond itself takes energy; more is released as the products form) to make GTP from GDP + Pi (substrate-level phosphorylation). The other three are oxidations that make NADH or FADH2, which give ATP only later through electron transport.
x: Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate is an oxidative decarboxylation that makes NADH and CO<sub>2</sub>, not GTP.
Succinate → fumarate makes FADH<sub>2</sub>, which yields ATP only later through electron transport.
Malate → oxaloacetate makes NADH, which yields ATP only later through electron transport.

q: Use the citric acid cycle shown. Which list contains ONLY steps that reduce NAD<sup>+</sup> to NADH?
c: isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate; α-ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA; malate → oxaloacetate
citrate → isocitrate; succinate → fumarate; malate → oxaloacetate
isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate; succinate → fumarate; fumarate → malate
α-ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA; succinyl CoA → succinate; fumarate → malate
h: Find each NADH on the wheel and note the conversion it comes from.
w: The three NADH come from the two oxidative decarboxylations (isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate, α-ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA) and malate → oxaloacetate. Succinate → fumarate uses FAD; citrate → isocitrate is an isomerization and fumarate → malate a hydration; succinyl CoA → succinate makes GTP.
x: Citrate → isocitrate is an isomerization, and succinate → fumarate reduces FAD, not NAD<sup>+</sup>.
Succinate → fumarate reduces FAD, and fumarate → malate is a hydration with no coenzyme.
Succinyl CoA → succinate makes GTP, and fumarate → malate is a hydration. Neither reduces NAD<sup>+</sup>.

q: Electrons from NADH travel through the electron transport chain. Which sequence shows the correct path?
c: Complex I → CoQ → Complex III → cyt c → Complex IV → O<sub>2</sub>
Complex I → cyt c → Complex III → CoQ → Complex IV → O<sub>2</sub>
Complex II → CoQ → Complex IV → cyt c → Complex III → O<sub>2</sub>
O<sub>2</sub> → Complex IV → cyt c → Complex III → CoQ → Complex I
h: The two mobile carriers alternate with the complexes: one small lipid-soluble carrier after Complex I, one small protein after Complex III.
w: NADH gives electrons to Complex I; CoQ carries them to Complex III; cytochrome c carries them to Complex IV, which reduces O2 to water: I → CoQ → III → cyt c → IV → O2. Electrons flow toward O2, not away from it.
x: The two mobile carriers are swapped. The small lipid-soluble carrier picks up electrons from Complex I; the small protein comes later.
NADH enters at Complex I, not Complex II, and Complex III comes before Complex IV.
This sequence runs backward. Electrons flow from NADH toward O<sub>2</sub>, not away from it.

q: Which component of the electron transport chain transfers electrons but does NOT pump H<sup>+</sup> into the intermembrane space?
h: Three complexes act as proton pumps. The one that does not is the entry point for FADH<sub>2</sub> from succinate.
w: Complexes I, III and IV pump H+, building the proton gradient. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) only passes electrons from FADH2 to CoQ, so FADH2 electrons drive fewer protons across the membrane.
x: Complex I, the NADH entry point, is a proton pump. Look for the complex where FADH<sub>2</sub> electrons enter.
Complex III pumps H<sup>+</sup> as it passes electrons from CoQ to cytochrome c.
Complex IV pumps H<sup>+</sup> as it passes electrons to O<sub>2</sub>.

q: Lignoceric acid, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>22</sub>COOH, is a saturated 24-carbon fatty acid. Using the ATP values in the table (subtract the activation cost), how many ATP are produced by its complete oxidation?
h: Acetyl CoA = carbons ÷ 2; β-oxidation cycles = acetyl CoA − 1; each cycle gives 1 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>.
w: 24 C → 12 acetyl CoA × 10 = 120 ATP. Cycles = 11 → 11 NADH × 2.5 + 11 FADH2 × 1.5 = 44 ATP. Total = 120 + 44 − 2 = 162 ATP. 164 forgets the activation cost; 166 uses 12 cycles instead of 11; 197 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH2.
x: 164 forgets to subtract the 2 ATP spent activating the fatty acid.
166 uses 12 β-oxidation cycles. The number of cycles is one less than the number of acetyl CoA.
197 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use the values in the table.

q: Caprylic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>COOH, found in goat's milk, is completely broken down by β-oxidation. How many acetyl CoA, NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> are produced?
h: Count all carbons, including CH<sub>3</sub> and COOH. The last turn of the spiral releases two acetyl CoA at once.
w: CH3 + 6 CH2 + COOH = 8 C → 8/2 = 4 acetyl CoA. Cycles = 4 − 1 = 3, each giving 1 NADH and 1 FADH2: 4 acetyl CoA, 3 NADH, 3 FADH2. 4 NADH assumes one cycle per acetyl CoA.
x: 4 NADH and 4 FADH<sub>2</sub> assumes one cycle per acetyl CoA. The last cycle splits a 4-carbon unit into two acetyl CoA.
3 acetyl CoA would be only 6 carbons. Count all the carbons, including the CH<sub>3</sub> and the COOH.
8 is the number of carbons, not acetyl CoA. Each acetyl CoA holds 2 carbons.

q: In one turn of β-oxidation: (1) a C=C forms between C2 and C3, (2) water adds across that C=C, (3) the new –OH is oxidized to C=O, and (4) HS–CoA cuts off acetyl CoA. Which coenzymes are reduced in reactions 1 and 3?
h: FAD handles –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– → –CH=CH–; NAD<sup>+</sup> handles C–OH → C=O.
w: Reaction 1 turns –CH2–CH2– into –CH=CH–, the kind of oxidation done by FAD; reaction 3 turns an alcohol into a ketone, done by NAD+. So each turn makes 1 FADH2, 1 NADH and 1 acetyl CoA.
x: The coenzymes are swapped. Forming a C=C from –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– uses one coenzyme, and oxidizing an alcohol to C=O uses the other.
Reaction 3 oxidizes an alcohol to a C=O. That type of oxidation does not use FAD.
Reaction 1 forms a C=C from a –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– group. That type of oxidation does not use NAD<sup>+</sup>.

q: A child with an inherited carnitine deficiency becomes weak and has low blood glucose during fasting. Which process is directly impaired?
c: Moving fatty acyl groups into the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation
Emulsifying dietary fats in the small intestine
Activating fatty acids by attaching them to CoA in the cytosol
h: Fatty acids are activated in the cytosol, but β-oxidation enzymes are inside the mitochondria. What carries them across?
w: Carnitine shuttles fatty acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Without it, fatty acyl groups cannot enter the matrix for β-oxidation, so fasting cells burn more glucose instead. Activation to fatty acyl CoA happens before carnitine is needed; bile salts and chylomicrons are digestion and transport steps.
x: Emulsifying dietary fat is done by bile salts in the intestine, not by carnitine.
Activation to fatty acyl CoA happens in the cytosol before carnitine is needed, so it still works. The problem comes in the next step.
Chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the intestine. Carnitine works inside cells, at the mitochondrion.

q: Urea, H2N–CO–NH2, is made in the liver by the urea cycle shown. Carbamoyl phosphate is made from NH+4 and CO2. Where do the two nitrogen atoms of urea come from?
c: One from NH+4 (via carbamoyl phosphate) and one from aspartate
Each from NH+4 released by transamination
Each from the amino group of glutamine in the kidney
One from CO<sub>2</sub> (via carbamoyl phosphate) and one from ornithine
h: Look at the two nitrogen-containing compounds that enter the cycle. Which one is made from NH+4?
w: Carbamoyl phosphate (from NH+4 + CO2) supplies the first N, and aspartate supplies the second, leaving as fumarate. Transamination moves amino groups but does not release NH+4 (oxidative deamination does), and CO2 provides the carbon, not nitrogen.
x: Only one nitrogen comes from free NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, and transamination moves amino groups without releasing NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>. Look for the second nitrogen-carrying compound that enters the cycle.
Urea is made in the liver, not the kidney, and the cycle uses two different nitrogen sources.
CO<sub>2</sub> contains no nitrogen; it provides urea's carbon. Ornithine is regenerated each turn rather than giving up its nitrogen.

q: Acetyl CoA cannot be converted into a net amount of glucose. The carbon skeleton of leucine is degraded only to acetyl CoA and acetoacetyl CoA. How is leucine classified?
c: Ketogenic: it cannot be used to make a net amount of glucose
Glucogenic: it can be converted to oxaloacetate
Essential and glucogenic: it can enter gluconeogenesis
Ketogenic: it is converted directly into urea
h: Gluconeogenesis needs pyruvate or a citric acid cycle intermediate. Acetyl CoA's two carbons are lost as CO<sub>2</sub>.
w: Amino acids degraded to acetyl CoA or acetoacetyl CoA can form ketone bodies or fatty acids but not a net amount of glucose, so leucine is ketogenic. Glucogenic amino acids give pyruvate or citric acid cycle intermediates. Urea comes from the amino group, not the carbon skeleton.
x: Leucine's skeleton gives only acetyl CoA and acetoacetyl CoA, not oxaloacetate. Glucogenic amino acids give pyruvate or cycle intermediates.
Leucine is essential, but its carbon skeleton cannot enter gluconeogenesis, because acetyl CoA's carbons leave as CO<sub>2</sub>.
Urea comes from the amino group, not the carbon skeleton. Classification depends on what the skeleton becomes.

q: The hydrolysis of ATP is shown below (energy released per mole of ATP). How much energy is released when 0.50 mol of ATP is hydrolyzed?
h: Energy released = moles × energy per mole.
w: 0.50 mol × 7.3 kcal mol⁻¹ = 3.7 kcal (2 significant figures). 15 kcal comes from multiplying by 2 instead of 0.50; 0.068 kcal comes from dividing 0.50 by 7.3.
x: 7.3 kcal is the energy for 1 mol of ATP. You have only 0.50 mol.
15 kcal multiplies by 2 instead of by 0.50. Half a mole releases less than one mole.
0.068 kcal divides 0.50 by 7.3. Multiply the moles by the energy per mole instead.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts fatty acid synthesis (lipogenesis) with β-oxidation?
c: Lipogenesis occurs in the cytosol and uses NADPH; β-oxidation occurs in mitochondria and uses FAD and NAD<sup>+</sup>.
Lipogenesis occurs in mitochondria and uses FAD; β-oxidation occurs in the cytosol and uses NADPH.
Each occurs in mitochondria and uses NAD<sup>+</sup> as the main coenzyme.
Lipogenesis removes 2-carbon units as acetyl CoA; β-oxidation adds 2-carbon units from malonyl CoA.
h: Building pathways need a reducing agent; breakdown pathways need oxidizing agents. They are kept in different compartments.
w: Lipogenesis is anabolic: in the cytosol, 2-carbon units from malonyl CoA are added on the acyl carrier protein and reduced by NADPH. β-Oxidation is catabolic: in the mitochondrial matrix, FAD and NAD+ remove H as 2-carbon units leave as acetyl CoA. The last choice reverses the two pathways.
x: The two pathways are switched: building fatty acids uses a reducing coenzyme, and breakdown uses oxidizing ones, in different compartments.
The two pathways are kept in different compartments and use different coenzymes; building needs a reducing agent, breakdown needs oxidizing agents.
This reverses the pathways. Lipogenesis builds chains, and β-oxidation cuts them down.

q: Capric acid, a saturated 10-carbon fatty acid found in goat's milk, is completely oxidized. Using the ATP values in the table (subtract the activation cost), how many ATP are produced?
h: Find acetyl CoA (carbons ÷ 2) and β-oxidation cycles (acetyl CoA − 1). Each cycle gives 1 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>.
w: 5 acetyl CoA × 10 = 50; 4 cycles give 4 NADH × 2.5 = 10 and 4 FADH2 × 1.5 = 6. 50 + 10 + 6 − 2 = 64 ATP. 66 forgets the activation cost; 68 uses 5 cycles instead of 4; 114 uses 10 acetyl CoA (one per carbon instead of one per two carbons).
x: 66 forgets to subtract the 2 ATP spent activating the fatty acid.
68 uses 5 β-oxidation cycles. The number of cycles is one less than the number of acetyl CoA.
114 uses 10 acetyl CoA, one per carbon. Each acetyl CoA carries 2 carbons.

q: A bottle of sports drink provides 120 kcal, all from carbohydrate. Using 4 kcal g⁻¹ for carbohydrate, how many grams of carbohydrate does it contain?
h: Divide the energy by the energy value per gram for that type of food.
w: 120 kcal ÷ 4 kcal g⁻¹ = 30 g of carbohydrate. 13 g uses 9 kcal g⁻¹, which is the value for fat, and 480 g multiplies instead of dividing.
x: 13 g uses 9 kcal g⁻¹, the value for fat. This drink's energy comes from carbohydrate.
480 g multiplies the kcal by 4 instead of dividing. A larger mass would give far more energy.
120 is the number of kcal, not grams. Convert using the energy value per gram.

q: One glucose is completely oxidized to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O by glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, the citric acid cycle and electron transport. Using the ATP values in the table (count the NADH from glycolysis at the same value), what is the total ATP yield?
h: Tally per glucose: glycolysis (2 ATP, 2 NADH), 2 pyruvate → acetyl CoA (2 NADH), and two turns of the citric acid cycle (6 NADH, 2 FADH<sub>2</sub>, 2 GTP).
w: NADH: 2 + 2 + 6 = 10 × 2.5 = 25; FADH2: 2 × 1.5 = 3; ATP + GTP made directly: 2 + 2 = 4. Total = 32 ATP. 34 counts the 4 ATP made in glycolysis without subtracting the 2 invested; 36 and 38 come from the older 3 ATP/NADH and 2 ATP/FADH2 values.
x: 34 counts the 4 ATP made in glycolysis without subtracting the 2 ATP invested at the start.
36 is an older total based on 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use 2.5 and 1.5 from the table.
38 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use the values in the table.

q: A pathway chart labels four processes: (1) building glycogen from glucose, (2) splitting glucose into two pyruvate, (3) making new glucose from lactate, (4) cutting a fatty acid into acetyl CoA. Which ones break molecules down?
h: Catabolic pathways break large molecules into smaller ones and release energy. Anabolic pathways build molecules and use energy. Latin: genesis = making, lysis = splitting.
w: Glycolysis splits glucose and β-oxidation breaks down fatty acids, so 2 and 4 are catabolic. Glycogenesis (making glycogen) and gluconeogenesis (making new glucose) are anabolic.
x: Processes 1 and 3 both build molecules (genesis = making), so they are anabolic.
Process 1 builds glycogen from glucose, which is anabolic. Only one of these two breaks molecules down.
Process 3 makes new glucose from lactate, which is anabolic. Only one of these two breaks molecules down.

q: In glycolysis, fructose-6-phosphate is converted to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Which coenzyme change accompanies this step?
h: A second phosphate group is added. Where does a phosphate come from in metabolism?
w: Adding a phosphate group (phosphorylation) uses one ATP, which becomes ADP: ATP → ADP. No hydrogen is removed, so NAD+ and FAD are not involved; ADP → ATP happens in steps that release a phosphate.
x: ATP is made later in glycolysis, when a phosphate is released. In this step a phosphate is added to the sugar.
No hydrogen is removed here, so NAD<sup>+</sup> is not involved. A phosphate group is being added.
FAD is used when a C=C forms. This step adds a second phosphate group to the sugar.

q: In each pair below, a coenzyme changes from the first form to the second. In which pair does the coenzyme gain hydrogen and get reduced?
h: In biochemistry, reduction usually means gaining hydrogen atoms (with their electrons).
w: FAD gains two hydrogen atoms (2 H+ + 2 e−) to become FADH2, a reduction. NADH → NAD+ and FADH2 → FAD lose hydrogen (oxidation), and ATP hydrolysis is not a redox change.
x: NADH loses hydrogen to become NAD<sup>+</sup>, so it is oxidized, not reduced.
FADH<sub>2</sub> loses hydrogen to become FAD, which is an oxidation. Look for the form that gains H.
ATP hydrolysis transfers a phosphate group; it is not a redox change and involves no gain of hydrogen.

q: Transamination removes alanine's amino group and leaves pyruvate behind. On that basis, which label fits alanine?
c: glucogenic, because pyruvate can be used to make glucose
ketogenic, because pyruvate forms ketone bodies only
essential, because pyruvate cannot be made in the body
h: Amino acids whose skeletons become pyruvate or citric acid cycle intermediates can feed gluconeogenesis.
w: Pyruvate can be turned into glucose by gluconeogenesis, so alanine is glucogenic. Ketogenic amino acids are degraded only to acetyl CoA or acetoacetyl CoA, which cannot give a net gain of glucose.
x: Pyruvate does not form only ketone bodies; it can be made into glucose by gluconeogenesis.
Pyruvate is made in the body all the time from glucose. Being essential means the amino acid must come from the diet.
Pyruvate does not enter β-oxidation, which breaks down fatty acids. Think about what the liver can build from pyruvate.

q: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, blood glucose rises and the pancreas releases insulin. Which process does insulin stimulate in the liver and muscle?
h: Insulin signals that fuel is plentiful. Will the body store glucose or release more of it?
w: Insulin promotes storage, so liver and muscle make glycogen from glucose: glycogenesis. Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis raise blood glucose and are stimulated by glucagon between meals.
x: Glycogenolysis breaks glycogen down to raise blood glucose. It is stimulated by glucagon between meals.
Gluconeogenesis makes new glucose, which would raise blood glucose further. It is stimulated by glucagon, not insulin.
Ketogenesis happens when insulin is low, such as during fasting or uncontrolled diabetes.

q: After a glass of wine, alcohol dehydrogenase turns ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) into acetaldehyde (CH<sub>3</sub>CHO). Which coenzyme takes part?
c: NAD<sup>+</sup>, which is reduced to NADH
FAD, which is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>
NADH, which is oxidized to NAD<sup>+</sup>
ATP, which is hydrolyzed to ADP
h: An alcohol losing two H atoms to become a C=O is an oxidation. Which coenzyme handles C–O oxidations, and which handles C–C?
w: Oxidizing an alcohol to a carbonyl removes 2 H, which are accepted by NAD+ → NADH. FAD is used when a C–C single bond becomes a C=C double bond.
x: FAD is used when a C–C single bond becomes a C=C. Here an alcohol becomes a C=O.
NADH → NAD<sup>+</sup> accompanies a reduction. Ethanol → acetaldehyde removes two H atoms, so it is an oxidation.
No phosphate is transferred in this step. The alcohol loses two H atoms to a coenzyme.

q: When a sprinter's leg muscles contract, the energy released by ATP hydrolysis is converted mainly into which form of energy?
h: Muscle contraction makes the body move. What type of energy is associated with motion?
w: Muscle proteins use the chemical energy of ATP hydrolysis to slide past each other, producing movement: chemical energy becomes mechanical energy (with some lost as heat).
x: Nuclear energy comes from changes in atomic nuclei, as in a power plant. Muscle contraction involves no nuclear reactions.
Some organisms such as fireflies turn ATP energy into light, but muscles do not. Think about what muscles do.
Making glucose would store energy, not use it. A contracting muscle is doing work.

q: One glucose gives two acetyl CoA, and each one goes around the citric acid cycle shown. In total, how many NADH, FADH<sub>2</sub>, CO<sub>2</sub> and GTP do these two turns produce?
h: Count what one turn of the wheel releases, then remember one glucose sends two acetyl CoA around the cycle.
w: One turn releases 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 2 CO2 and 1 GTP. Two turns per glucose double each: 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 4 CO2, 2 GTP. "8 NADH, 6 CO2" also counts the pyruvate → acetyl CoA step, which is not part of the cycle.
x: These are the products of just one turn. One glucose sends two acetyl CoA around the cycle.
8 NADH and 6 CO<sub>2</sub> also count the pyruvate → acetyl CoA step, which happens before the cycle.
One turn makes only 1 FADH<sub>2</sub> and 1 GTP, so two turns give 2 of each.

q: In the citric acid cycle shown, which conversion is an oxidative decarboxylation?
h: An oxidative decarboxylation does two things at once: a coenzyme is reduced and a carbon leaves as CO<sub>2</sub>.
w: Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate releases both NADH and CO2: the substrate is oxidized (NAD+ → NADH) and loses a carbon as CO2. Succinate → fumarate is an oxidation (FAD) with no CO2; citrate → isocitrate is an isomerization; succinyl CoA → succinate makes GTP but neither oxidizes nor decarboxylates.
x: Succinate → fumarate is an oxidation by FAD, but no carbon is lost as CO<sub>2</sub>.
Citrate → isocitrate is an isomerization; the formula does not change and no coenzyme is reduced.
Succinyl CoA → succinate makes GTP. It is neither an oxidation nor a loss of CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: Acetyl CoA enters the cycle shown as indicated by the blue arrow. Which 4-carbon compound does the 2-carbon acetyl group combine with to form citrate (6 C)?
h: Find the compound that comes right before citrate in the wheel; it is regenerated at the end of every turn.
w: Citrate (6 C) = acetyl group (2 C) + oxaloacetate (4 C). Oxaloacetate is the last compound of the wheel, so it is regenerated each turn, which is why the pathway is a cycle. Succinyl CoA, succinate and fumarate are also 4-carbon compounds, but they come earlier in the cycle and do not react with acetyl CoA.
x: Succinate is a 4-carbon compound in the middle of the cycle. It does not react with acetyl CoA.
Succinyl CoA forms after a CO<sub>2</sub> is lost, partway around the cycle. It does not react with acetyl CoA.
Fumarate is a 4-carbon compound late in the cycle, but it is hydrated to malate rather than joined to acetyl CoA.

q: In the citric acid cycle shown, the reduced coenzyme labeled X is formed when succinate is converted to fumarate. What is X, and why is this coenzyme used here?
c: FADH<sub>2</sub>; a C–C single bond is oxidized to a C=C double bond
NADH; a C–OH group is oxidized to a C=O group
FADH<sub>2</sub>; a C–OH group is oxidized to a C=O group
NADH; a C–C single bond is oxidized to a C=C double bond
h: Compare the structures: succinate is a saturated chain; fumarate has a C=C. Which coenzyme handles alkane → alkene oxidations?
w: Succinate → fumarate removes 2 H from neighboring carbons and makes a C=C, the type of oxidation done by FAD, so X = FADH2. NAD+ is used when C–OH is oxidized to C=O, as in malate → oxaloacetate.
x: Succinate has no C–OH group, and NAD<sup>+</sup> is not the coenzyme here. Compare the two structures: what new bond forms?
Succinate has no C–OH group. Compare the structures to see what new bond forms.
A C=C does form here, but that type of oxidation does not use NAD<sup>+</sup>.

q: Four acetyl CoA from the breakdown of a fatty acid go through the citric acid cycle shown. How many NADH and how many CO<sub>2</sub> are produced?
h: Read the NADH and CO<sub>2</sub> released in one trip around the wheel; each acetyl CoA makes one trip.
w: One turn: 3 NADH and 2 CO2. Four turns: 4 × 3 = 12 NADH and 4 × 2 = 8 CO2, so 12 NADH and 8 CO2. Each turn releases both carbons of the acetyl group as CO2; 16 NADH wrongly adds a pyruvate dehydrogenase NADH, which fatty acid acetyl CoA never passes through.
x: Each turn makes 3 NADH, not 1. Count the NADH released in one trip around the wheel.
Each turn releases 2 CO<sub>2</sub>, both carbons of the acetyl group, not just 1.
16 NADH adds a pyruvate → acetyl CoA NADH for each acetyl CoA. Acetyl CoA from a fatty acid never goes through that step.

q: Glycolysis is shown. For one glucose, what are the net yields of ATP and NADH?
h: Add up the ATP made, then subtract the ATP invested in the early steps.
w: ATP made: 2 + 2 = 4; ATP invested: 1 + 1 = 2; net = 2 ATP. NADH: 2 (one from each glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate). "4 ATP" forgets the 2 ATP spent in the energy-investment steps.
x: 4 ATP is the gross amount made. Subtract the 2 ATP spent in the energy-investment steps.
Glucose splits into two 3-carbon pieces, and each one is oxidized once, so the NADH count is not 1.
4 ATP forgets the ATP invested, and only one step per 3-carbon piece makes NADH.

q: In the glycolysis pathway shown, two labels are hidden. What are Y and Z?
h: Y goes in and ADP comes out at the same step. Z forms when NAD<sup>+</sup> goes in.
w: Steps 1 and 3 are the energy-investment steps: a phosphate group is transferred from ATP, leaving ADP. When glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate is oxidized, 2 NAD+ are reduced to 2 NADH. Glycolysis makes no FADH2 and releases no CO2.
x: ADP comes out of these steps, so it cannot also be what goes in. The phosphate donor must be the higher-energy form.
Glycolysis makes no FADH<sub>2</sub>. The oxidation of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate uses a different coenzyme.
Glycolysis releases no CO<sub>2</sub>; all six carbons end up in the two pyruvates. Z forms when a coenzyme is reduced.

q: A muscle cell breaks down 3 glucose molecules by the pathway shown. How many pyruvate and how many net ATP form?
h: Find the yield per glucose from the pathway, then multiply by the number of glucose molecules.
w: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvate and a net 2 ATP. For 3 glucose: 3 × 2 = 6 pyruvate and 3 × 2 = 6 ATP. 12 ATP is the gross yield, before subtracting the 6 ATP invested.
x: Each glucose splits into 2 pyruvate, so 3 glucose give more than 3 pyruvate.
12 ATP is the gross yield. Subtract the 6 ATP invested in the early steps for 3 glucose.
3 ATP is the net yield for only 1.5 glucose. Multiply the net per-glucose yield by 3.

q: During a sprint, muscle cells run low on O<sub>2</sub> and carry out the pathway shown. What is the main purpose of the last step, pyruvate → lactate?
c: to regenerate NAD<sup>+</sup> so that glycolysis can continue
to make 2 more ATP for each glucose
to convert pyruvate into acetyl CoA for the citric acid cycle
to release CO<sub>2</sub> so that the muscle cells stay neutral
h: Follow the NADH made in glycolysis. What happens to it in the last step, and why would glycolysis need that?
w: Glycolysis needs NAD+ to oxidize glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. Without O2, NADH cannot be reoxidized by electron transport, so pyruvate is reduced to lactate and NAD+ is regenerated. The step makes no ATP and releases no CO2; acetyl CoA forms only under aerobic conditions.
x: Pyruvate → lactate makes no ATP. Follow what happens to the NADH made earlier in glycolysis.
Acetyl CoA forms only when oxygen is plentiful. Here O<sub>2</sub> is low and pyruvate becomes lactate.
Pyruvate → lactate releases no CO<sub>2</sub>; both have 3 carbons. Think about which coenzyme is changed.

q: For one glucose, both pyruvate molecules go through the step shown. How many CO<sub>2</sub> and NADH are produced in this step?
h: Each pyruvate makes the trip once. One glucose gives how many pyruvate?
w: One glucose → 2 pyruvate. Each pyruvate → acetyl CoA releases 1 CO2 and 1 NADH, so the total is 2 CO2 and 2 NADH. "1 and 1" is per pyruvate, not per glucose; 6 CO2 is the total for complete oxidation of glucose.
x: 1 CO<sub>2</sub> and 1 NADH is the yield for one pyruvate. One glucose gives two pyruvate.
Each pyruvate gives one CO<sub>2</sub> and one NADH, so the two counts must be equal.
6 CO<sub>2</sub> is the total for complete oxidation of glucose. This single step releases only some of them.

q: Using the pathway and the ATP value in the table, how many ATP in total come from converting one glucose into two acetyl CoA (count the ATP made directly plus the ATP made when all the NADH shown is oxidized)?
h: Add the NADH from both steps, multiply by its ATP value, then add the ATP made directly in glycolysis.
w: NADH: 2 (glycolysis) + 2 (pyruvate oxidation) = 4; 4 × 2.5 = 10 ATP. Add the 2 net ATP from glycolysis: 12 ATP. 7 counts only the glycolysis NADH (5 + 2); 10 forgets the 2 ATP made directly; 2 counts only the ATP made directly and ignores the NADH.
x: 7 counts the glycolysis NADH and the 2 ATP made directly, but leaves out the 2 NADH from pyruvate oxidation shown in the second step.
10 counts all the NADH but forgets the 2 net ATP made directly in glycolysis.
2 counts only the ATP made directly in glycolysis. The NADH must also be converted to ATP.

q: Stearic acid (18 C) is activated to stearoyl CoA and broken down completely by the β-oxidation spiral shown. How many times does the spiral turn, and how many acetyl CoA are produced?
h: Each turn cuts off 2 carbons. The last turn splits a 4-carbon unit into two acetyl CoA.
w: 18 C ÷ 2 = 9 acetyl CoA. The final turn produces two acetyl CoA at once, so the number of turns is one less: 8 turns. "9 turns" forgets that the last 4-carbon piece gives two acetyl CoA in one turn.
x: 9 turns forgets that the last turn splits a 4-carbon piece into two acetyl CoA at once.
8 turns is right, but the last turn releases two acetyl CoA. Divide the carbons by 2 for the acetyl CoA count.
18 acetyl CoA counts one per carbon; each acetyl CoA has 2 carbons. The turn count is also one too many.

q: Myristic acid (14 C), found in coconut oil and nutmeg, is broken down completely by the β-oxidation spiral shown. How many NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> does β-oxidation itself produce (not counting the citric acid cycle)?
h: Each turn of the spiral gives one NADH and one FADH<sub>2</sub>. How many turns does a 14-carbon acid need?
w: 14 C → 7 acetyl CoA, made in 7 − 1 = 6 turns. Each turn gives 1 FADH2 and 1 NADH: 6 NADH and 6 FADH2. "7 and 7" uses the number of acetyl CoA instead of the number of turns.
x: 7 and 7 uses the number of acetyl CoA instead of the number of turns. The last turn gives two acetyl CoA.
13 is far more turns than a 14-carbon chain needs. Each turn removes 2 carbons, not 1.
Every turn makes one FADH<sub>2</sub> in its first step, when a C=C forms. FADH<sub>2</sub> cannot be zero.

q: Lauric acid (12 C), the main fatty acid in coconut oil, is oxidized by the spiral shown and the citric acid cycle. Using the ATP values in the table, what is the net ATP yield?
h: Find the acetyl CoA (C ÷ 2) and the turns (one fewer). Each turn gives 1 NADH and 1 FADH<sub>2</sub>; subtract the activation cost.
w: 6 acetyl CoA × 10 = 60; 5 turns → 5 NADH × 2.5 = 12.5 and 5 FADH2 × 1.5 = 7.5. Total 60 + 12.5 + 7.5 − 2 = 78 ATP. 80 forgets the 2-ATP activation cost; 82 uses 6 turns instead of 5; 95 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH2.
x: 80 forgets to subtract the 2 ATP spent activating the fatty acid.
82 uses 6 turns. The number of turns is one less than the number of acetyl CoA.
95 uses the older values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use the values in the table.

q: Arachidic acid, a saturated 20-carbon fatty acid in peanut oil, is oxidized by the spiral shown and every acetyl CoA then goes through the citric acid cycle (3 NADH per acetyl CoA). How many NADH form in total?
h: Add two sources: the NADH from the turns of the spiral and the NADH from the acetyl CoA in the citric acid cycle.
w: 20 C → 10 acetyl CoA in 9 turns. β-Oxidation: 9 NADH. Citric acid cycle: 10 × 3 = 30 NADH. Total = 39 NADH. 36 sends only 9 acetyl CoA through the cycle (confusing turns with acetyl CoA); 9 and 30 each count only one of the two sources.
x: 9 counts only the NADH from the β-oxidation turns. The acetyl CoA also make NADH in the citric acid cycle.
30 counts only the NADH from the citric acid cycle. Add the NADH made in the β-oxidation turns.
36 sends only 9 acetyl CoA through the cycle, confusing turns with acetyl CoA. A 20-carbon acid gives 10 acetyl CoA.

q: A 14-carbon fatty acyl CoA has gone around the β-oxidation spiral shown three times. How many carbons are left in the shortened fatty acyl CoA, and how many acetyl CoA have been released so far?
h: Look at the last step: each turn removes a 2-carbon unit as one acetyl CoA.
w: Each turn releases one acetyl CoA (2 C). After 3 turns: 14 − 3 × 2 = 8 C remain, with 3 acetyl CoA released. "11 C" removes only 1 carbon per turn; "6 acetyl CoA" counts 2 per turn.
x: Each turn cuts off a 2-carbon acetyl unit, not 1 carbon. Subtract 2 carbons for every turn.
Each turn releases just one acetyl CoA (one 2-carbon piece). Six acetyl CoA would mean two per turn.
This counts one turn too many. Three turns remove three 2-carbon units; check the carbon count and acetyl CoA count again.

q: Electrons flow through the electron transport chain shown. What is the final electron acceptor at the position marked "?"
c: O<sub>2</sub>, which is reduced to H<sub>2</sub>O
NAD<sup>+</sup>, which is reduced to NADH
H<sub>2</sub>O, which is oxidized to O<sub>2</sub>
CO<sub>2</sub>, which is reduced to glucose
h: Why do we need to breathe? The last carrier hands its electrons to something we inhale.
w: Complex IV passes the electrons to O2, which picks up H+ and is reduced to H2O. This is why aerobic metabolism needs O2. NAD+ is reduced at the start of the process (in the citric acid cycle), not at the end of the chain.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced earlier, in pathways like the citric acid cycle. At the end of the chain, electrons go to a gas we breathe in.
This runs backward: water splitting into O<sub>2</sub> happens in photosynthesis. In our cells the last carrier hands electrons to something that becomes water.
Reducing CO<sub>2</sub> to glucose is photosynthesis in plants. Human cells release CO<sub>2</sub>; they do not use it to accept electrons.

q: In the electron transport chain shown, electrons from FADH<sub>2</sub> enter through complex II and go directly to coenzyme Q. Why does each FADH<sub>2</sub> give fewer ATP (1.5) than each NADH (2.5)?
c: Its electrons bypass complex I, so fewer H<sup>+</sup> are pumped
Its electrons go to O<sub>2</sub> without passing complex IV
FADH<sub>2</sub> carries only one electron instead of two
FADH<sub>2</sub> makes ATP only by substrate-level phosphorylation
h: Count the H<sup>+</sup> pumping steps each type of electron passes through on the way to O<sub>2</sub>.
w: NADH electrons pass all three pumping sites (complexes I, III and IV). FADH2 electrons enter at coenzyme Q, skipping complex I, so fewer H+ are pumped and ATP synthase makes less ATP. Both carriers deliver 2 electrons, and both still pass through complex IV to O2.
x: Electrons from FADH<sub>2</sub> still pass through complex IV on their way to O<sub>2</sub>. Look at where they enter the chain instead.
FADH<sub>2</sub> and NADH each deliver 2 electrons. The difference is in how many H<sup>+</sup> pumping complexes those electrons pass through.
FADH<sub>2</sub> feeds the electron transport chain, so its ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation. Substrate-level phosphorylation does not use FADH<sub>2</sub>.

q: In the electron transport chain shown, carrier X accepts electrons from both complex I (from NADH) and complex II (from FADH2) and passes them to complex III. What is X?
