h: X is a small mobile carrier that sits between complexes I/II and complex III.
w: Both NADH (via complex I) and FADH2 (via complex II) hand their electrons to coenzyme Q (ubiquinone), which carries them to complex III. Cytochrome c is the carrier between complexes III and IV; ATP synthase makes ATP but does not carry electrons.
x: Cytochrome c shuttles electrons later in the chain, between complexes III and IV. X sits before complex III.
ATP synthase uses the H<sup>+</sup> gradient to make ATP; it does not carry electrons between complexes.
NAD<sup>+</sup> is the oxidized form left after NADH gives up its electrons at complex I. It does not carry electrons on to complex III.

q: In the urea cycle shown (in the liver), which compound is released at the step marked "?" and carried by the blood to the kidneys for excretion?
h: This is the step that splits arginine and regenerates ornithine, so the cycle can start again.
w: Arginine is hydrolyzed to urea, which is excreted in urine, and ornithine, which starts the next turn. Fumarate leaves at the earlier step, NH+4 is the toxic waste the cycle removes, and aspartate enters the cycle.
x: Fumarate leaves at an earlier step, when argininosuccinate is split. It goes to the citric acid cycle, not to the kidneys.
NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is the toxic waste the cycle is designed to get rid of. The cycle converts it into a safer compound before it leaves the liver.
Aspartate enters the cycle, bringing in a nitrogen. It is not released at the step that regenerates ornithine.

q: Each turn of the urea cycle shown makes one urea, H<sub>2</sub>N–CO–NH<sub>2</sub>. If a patient's liver excretes 12 nitrogen atoms as urea, how many turns of the cycle occur, and how many aspartate molecules enter?
h: Count the N atoms in one urea. One N comes from carbamoyl phosphate and one from aspartate in each turn.
w: Each urea carries 2 N, so 12 N ÷ 2 = 6 turns (one urea per turn). One aspartate enters per turn, supplying one of the two N, so 6 aspartate are used. "12 turns" forgets that each urea removes two N atoms at once.
x: This assumes one N per urea. Look at H<sub>2</sub>N–CO–NH<sub>2</sub>: each urea carries two N atoms, so fewer turns are needed.
The turns are right, but only one aspartate enters per turn. The other N comes from carbamoyl phosphate.
This assumes one N per urea for the turns. Each urea carries two N, and one aspartate enters per turn, so the two numbers should match.

q: In the urea cycle shown, one product leaves the cycle and can enter the citric acid cycle, linking the two pathways. Which compound is it?
h: Which product of the urea cycle is also an intermediate in the citric acid cycle?
w: Argininosuccinate is split into arginine and fumarate. Fumarate is also an intermediate of the citric acid cycle (fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate), so it links the two cycles. Urea is excreted, and citrulline and carbamoyl phosphate stay within the urea cycle.
x: Urea is the waste product carried to the kidneys and excreted. It is not a citric acid cycle intermediate.
Citrulline stays within the urea cycle; it reacts with aspartate in the next step. It is not part of the citric acid cycle.
Carbamoyl phosphate is the entry compound that brings NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> into the urea cycle. It does not leave to join the citric acid cycle.

q: A liver cell is making glycogen from glucose and proteins from amino acids. Which statement correctly describes these anabolic pathways?
c: They build larger molecules from smaller ones and generally require ATP
They break large molecules into smaller ones and release energy
They oxidize fuels to CO<sub>2</sub> and reduce NAD<sup>+</sup> to NADH
They occur only in the mitochondria during fasting
h: Ana- = building up; cata- = breaking down. Building bonds costs energy.
w: Anabolism is biosynthesis: small molecules are joined into larger ones (glucose → glycogen, amino acids → protein, acetyl CoA → fatty acids), which requires energy from ATP and usually reducing power (NADPH). Breaking fuels down to CO2 while making NADH describes catabolism.
x: Breaking large molecules down and releasing energy describes catabolism. Making glycogen and proteins builds things up.
Oxidizing fuels to CO<sub>2</sub> while making NADH is catabolism. Building pathways usually use reducing power and ATP instead.
Building pathways like glycogen and protein synthesis run in many places, mostly when fuel is plentiful (after a meal), not only during fasting.

q: Which metabolic term means "the synthesis of new glucose from non-carbohydrate molecules such as lactate or amino acids"?
h: Break the word apart: gluco- (glucose), neo- (new), -genesis (creation).
w: Gluconeogenesis = "new glucose creation", mainly in the liver during fasting. Glycogenolysis is the splitting (-lysis) of glycogen into glucose, glycolysis is the splitting of glucose into pyruvate and glycogenesis is making glycogen from glucose.
x: Glycogenolysis is the splitting (-lysis) of glycogen into glucose units. That starts from a stored carbohydrate, not from lactate or amino acids.
Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate. It breaks glucose down rather than making new glucose.
Glycogenesis makes glycogen from glucose. It does not create new glucose from non-carbohydrate molecules.

q: After a large meal, the liver converts excess glucose into glycogen for storage. Which term names this process, and is it anabolic or catabolic?
h: -genesis means making; -lysis means splitting. Making a polymer from monomers builds up, so which category is that?
w: Joining glucose units into the polymer glycogen is glycogenesis, a building (anabolic) process that uses ATP. Glycogenolysis is the reverse breakdown; glycolysis breaks glucose into pyruvate; gluconeogenesis is anabolic but makes glucose, not glycogen.
x: Glycogenolysis breaks glycogen down into glucose: the opposite of storing excess glucose.
Glycolysis breaks glucose into pyruvate for energy. The liver here is storing glucose as a polymer.
Gluconeogenesis is anabolic, but it makes new glucose from non-carbohydrates. Here glucose is being turned into a storage polymer.

q: The last step of the citric acid cycle, malate → oxaloacetate, is drawn. Which coenzyme is required, and what happens to it?
c: NAD<sup>+</sup>, which is reduced to NADH
FAD, which is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>
NADH, which is oxidized to NAD<sup>+</sup>
Coenzyme A, which accepts the acetyl group
h: An alcohol is being oxidized to a ketone. Which coenzyme picks up hydrogen from an alcohol or aldehyde, and which from a –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– group?
w: The secondary alcohol –CH(OH)– loses two hydrogens to become a C=O: an oxidation. Oxidations of alcohols and aldehydes use NAD+, which is reduced to NADH (later worth about 2.5 ATP). FAD is reserved for oxidizing a C–C single bond to a C=C double bond, as in succinate → fumarate.
x: FAD handles C–C single bond → C=C double bond oxidations, like succinate → fumarate. Here an alcohol becomes a ketone.
Malate is losing hydrogens here (oxidized), so the coenzyme must gain them. NADH being oxidized would mean hydrogens are added to the substrate.
Coenzyme A carries acyl groups and accepts no hydrogen. This step is an oxidation of an alcohol to a ketone.

q: After alcohol is consumed, the liver converts acetaldehyde to acetate as drawn. Which description of this step is correct?
c: Oxidation of an aldehyde; NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced to NADH
Reduction of an aldehyde; NADH is oxidized to NAD<sup>+</sup>
h: Compare the carbon in question: an aldehyde carbon becomes a carboxylate carbon. Does it gain oxygen or hydrogen?
w: The –CHO carbon gains an oxygen (and loses its H) to become –COO−, so acetaldehyde is oxidized; the electrons and hydrogen go to NAD+, forming NADH. This is why heavy drinking floods the liver with NADH. No CO2 leaves and no bond is split by water.
x: The aldehyde carbon gains an oxygen to become a carboxylate, which is oxidation, not reduction. Check which way the coenzyme changes too.
Hydrolysis splits a molecule into two pieces using water. Both structures here have two carbons; only the end carbon changed.
Decarboxylation removes a carbon as CO<sub>2</sub>. Both molecules have two carbons, so no carbon was lost.

q: In the step of the citric acid cycle drawn, succinate loses two hydrogen atoms to become fumarate. Which coenzyme picks up those hydrogen atoms?
h: Look at what changed: a –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– became a –CH=CH–. One specific coenzyme handles this kind of oxidation.
w: Oxidizing a saturated C–C bond to a C=C double bond (removing 2 H) is the job of FAD, which is reduced to FADH2 (later worth about 1.5 ATP). NAD+ handles alcohol → carbonyl oxidations. Coenzyme A carries acyl groups and ATP transfers phosphate; neither accepts hydrogen.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> usually oxidizes alcohols and aldehydes to C=O groups. Here a –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– became a C=C double bond.
Coenzyme A carries acyl groups such as acetyl; it does not accept hydrogen atoms from the substrate.
ATP transfers phosphate groups and does not accept hydrogen atoms. Also, ATP → ADP is a phosphate change, not a reduction.

q: Fat cells attach a phosphate group to glycerol, as drawn, before building triacylglycerols. Which coenzyme change goes along with this phosphorylation?
h: A phosphate group was added to the molecule. Where does a cell get a phosphate group it can donate?
w: Adding a phosphate group to a molecule (phosphorylation) uses ATP as the phosphate donor, leaving ADP. "ADP → ATP" is the reverse: it describes a step that makes ATP by removing a phosphate from a substrate. No hydrogen is removed, so NAD+ and FAD are not involved.
x: ADP → ATP happens when a phosphate is removed from a substrate. Here the glycerol gains a phosphate, so the donor loses one.
NAD<sup>+</sup> → NADH goes with an oxidation (hydrogen removed). Glycerol keeps all its hydrogens and simply gains a phosphate.
FAD → FADH<sub>2</sub> goes with forming a C=C double bond. No hydrogen is removed here; a phosphate group is added.

q: A sprinter's oxygen-starved leg muscle carries out the reaction drawn, turning pyruvate into lactate. Which label describes what happens to pyruvate?
c: Reduction; NADH is oxidized to NAD<sup>+</sup>
Oxidation; NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced to NADH
Hydration; H<sub>2</sub>O adds to the C=O
Decarboxylation; a carbon is lost as CO<sub>2</sub>
h: Compare the middle carbon: a ketone C=O becomes –CH(OH)–. Did the molecule gain or lose hydrogen?
w: The ketone gains two hydrogen atoms to become a secondary alcohol, so pyruvate is reduced; the hydrogens come from NADH, which is oxidized back to NAD+ so glycolysis can continue. Both molecules keep three carbons, so there is no decarboxylation, and no water is added.
x: Compare the middle carbon: the C=O becomes –CH(OH)–, so pyruvate gains hydrogen. The arrow also shows NADH turning into NAD<sup>+</sup>.
Hydration would add H<sub>2</sub>O. Here two hydrogen atoms come from a coenzyme, as shown over the arrow.
Decarboxylation would lose a carbon. Both pyruvate and lactate have three carbons.

q: In yeast, pyruvate is converted to acetaldehyde as drawn (the step before ethanol forms). How is this reaction labeled?
c: Oxidation; NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced to NADH
h: Count carbons on each side. Three became two: the small molecule written over the arrow left.
w: Pyruvate (3 C) loses its carboxylate carbon as CO2, leaving acetaldehyde (2 C): a decarboxylation. No hydrogen is removed, so NAD+ is not reduced here (it is NADH that then reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol). Water is neither removed nor added.
x: An oxidation removes hydrogen or adds oxygen. Here no hydrogen is removed; count the carbons and look at what is written over the arrow.
Dehydration removes H<sub>2</sub>O. The small molecule over the arrow is CO<sub>2</sub>, and a carbon was lost.
Hydrolysis uses water to split a bond. No water is added here; a carbon leaves as a gas.

q: Which coenzyme carries the two-carbon acetyl group from pyruvate (or from β-oxidation) into the citric acid cycle?
h: The acetyl group is attached through a thioester bond to a coenzyme made from vitamin B<sub>5</sub>.
w: Coenzyme A (HS–CoA) bonds to the acetyl group through its –SH, forming acetyl CoA, which delivers the two carbons to oxaloacetate to make citrate. NAD+ and FAD carry hydrogen (electrons); ATP carries phosphate groups.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> carries hydrogen (electrons), not carbon groups. The acetyl carrier links to the acetyl group through a sulfur atom.
FAD carries hydrogen (electrons), not carbon groups. Think of a coenzyme that forms a thioester with the acetyl group.
ATP carries phosphate groups and energy, not acetyl groups. The carrier you want is made from vitamin B5.

q: NADH delivers its electrons to complex I of the electron transport chain. In this step NADH is ____ and complex I is ____.
h: LEO says GER: Losing Electrons is Oxidation; Gaining Electrons is Reduction. NADH gives electrons away.
w: NADH loses two electrons (and H+) and becomes NAD+, so it is oxidized; complex I gains those electrons, so it is reduced. The electrons then pass down the chain to O2, each carrier being reduced then re-oxidized. Students often reverse this because NADH is "the reduced coenzyme", but it gets oxidized when it unloads.
x: NADH is the reduced form, but here it gives its electrons away. Losing electrons is oxidation, and whatever gains them is reduced.
Electrons cannot just disappear: if NADH loses them, complex I must gain them. Both cannot be oxidized.
NADH loses electrons in this step, so it cannot be the one being reduced. Use LEO says GER.

q: Glycolysis produces 2 NADH per glucose in the cytosol. What must happen to these NADH before their energy appears as ATP?
c: Their electrons must be shuttled into the mitochondria to the electron transport chain
They are hydrolyzed in the cytosol, releasing their stored energy directly as ATP
They donate their hydrogen atoms to pyruvate, converting it into acetyl CoA
They diffuse out of the muscle cell and are excreted in the urine unchanged
h: Where is the electron transport chain located? NADH is only "worth" ATP when O<sub>2</sub> takes its electrons.
w: The electron transport chain and ATP synthase are in the inner mitochondrial membrane, so cytosolic NADH must pass its electrons (via a shuttle) into the mitochondria, where NADH is oxidized to NAD+ and the energy drives ATP synthesis (about 2.5 ATP each by the malate–aspartate shuttle, or 1.5 by the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle). NADH cannot be hydrolyzed for ATP, and pyruvate → acetyl CoA produces NADH rather than using it.
x: NADH is not hydrolyzed like ATP. Its energy is released only when its electrons are passed along a chain to O<sub>2</sub>.
Pyruvate → acetyl CoA actually produces NADH; it does not use it. Think about where the electron transport chain is located.
NADH is a recycled coenzyme, not a waste product. Its electrons are used to make ATP inside the cell.

q: When a cyclist pedals, ATP made from the oxidation of glucose is used by muscle proteins. Which energy conversion best describes muscle contraction?
c: Chemical energy in ATP → mechanical energy of movement (plus heat)
Mechanical energy → chemical energy stored in glycogen
Light energy → chemical energy in ATP
Electrical energy → chemical energy in NADH
h: The energy was stored in chemical bonds of food, then of ATP. What form does it take when a muscle shortens?
w: Hydrolysis of ATP releases chemical energy, which myosin converts into mechanical work as the muscle fibers slide, with much of the rest lost as heat (why exercise warms you). Storing glycogen is chemical → chemical; light → chemical is photosynthesis.
x: This is backward. During contraction, energy stored in ATP is spent to move the muscle, not stored in glycogen.
Light → chemical energy happens in photosynthesis in plants. Muscle runs on ATP made from food.
Muscle contraction does not make NADH. The energy in ATP is used to produce movement and heat.

q: In the citric acid cycle drawn, one intermediate has been replaced by a question mark. Which compound is missing?
h: The hidden compound has 5 carbons: it forms when isocitrate (6 C) loses CO<sub>2</sub>, and it loses another CO<sub>2</sub> to give succinyl CoA (4 C).
w: Isocitrate (6 C) undergoes oxidative decarboxylation to α-ketoglutarate (5 C), which is then decarboxylated again to succinyl CoA (4 C); the two CO2 on the arrows confirm it. Pyruvate is converted to acetyl CoA before the cycle, acetoacetate is a ketone body and glucose 6-phosphate belongs to glycolysis, so none of them is an intermediate of the cycle.
x: Pyruvate is changed to acetyl CoA before the cycle starts, so it is not a cycle intermediate. The missing compound has 5 carbons.
Acetoacetate is a ketone body made in the liver during fasting. It is not one of the citric acid cycle intermediates.
Glucose 6-phosphate belongs to glycolysis (and glycogen metabolism). The missing cycle intermediate has 5 carbons.

q: Before a fatty acid can be oxidized it is "activated" by attaching coenzyme A, a step in which ATP is converted to AMP and two phosphates. What is the energy cost of activation?
c: No ATP; the step releases energy
h: ATP → AMP breaks two phosphate bonds, not one. Count how many ATP it takes to rebuild ATP from AMP.
w: Activation hydrolyzes ATP to AMP + PPi, breaking two high-energy phosphate bonds; restoring AMP to ATP costs two phosphorylations, so the cost is counted as 2 ATP. This is why the total ATP from a fatty acid is reduced by 2 (for example 108 − 2 = 106 for palmitic acid). A hexokinase-type phosphorylation (ATP → ADP) would cost only 1.
x: Activation uses one ATP molecule, but it goes all the way to AMP, breaking two phosphate bonds. Count how much it costs to rebuild ATP from AMP.
This double-counts. ATP → AMP breaks two high-energy phosphate bonds, and each bond is counted as one ATP.
Activation costs energy: ATP is broken down to AMP to attach coenzyme A. That is why the fatty acid's total ATP yield is reduced.

q: Each turn of the β-oxidation spiral shown produces one NADH and one FADH2 (plus an acetyl CoA that enters the citric acid cycle separately). Using 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH2, how many ATP come from the coenzymes of one turn?
h: Add the ATP value of one NADH to the ATP value of one FADH<sub>2</sub>; ignore the acetyl CoA for this question.
w: One turn: 1 NADH × 2.5 + 1 FADH2 × 1.5 = 4 ATP. "2.5" counts only the NADH, "5" uses the old value of 2 ATP per FADH2 plus 3 per NADH, and "14" adds the 10 ATP from the acetyl CoA going through the citric acid cycle.
x: That counts only the NADH. One turn also produces an FADH<sub>2</sub>, which is worth ATP too.
This uses the old values of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH<sub>2</sub>. Use 2.5 and 1.5 as stated in the question.
This adds the 10 ATP from the acetyl CoA going through the citric acid cycle. The question asks only about the coenzymes from the spiral itself.

q: Palmitoyl CoA (16 carbons) goes completely through the β-oxidation spiral shown. Using 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH2, how many ATP are produced from the NADH and FADH2 of the spiral itself (not counting the acetyl CoA or the activation cost)?
h: Find the number of turns first (one fewer than the number of acetyl CoA), then multiply by the ATP from one turn's NADH + FADH<sub>2</sub>.
w: 16 C gives 8 acetyl CoA in 16/2 − 1 = 7 turns. Each turn yields 1 NADH (2.5) + 1 FADH2 (1.5) = 4 ATP, so 7 × 4 = 28 ATP. "32" uses 8 turns, "20" counts only the NADH and uses 8 turns (8 × 2.5), and "106" is the total yield including the 8 acetyl CoA minus activation.
x: This uses 8 turns. A 16-carbon chain gives 8 acetyl CoA in only 7 turns, because the last turn splits a 4-carbon piece into two acetyl CoA.
This counts only the NADH (and uses 8 turns). Each turn also makes an FADH<sub>2</sub>, worth 1.5 ATP.
106 is the total ATP for palmitate, including the acetyl CoA and the activation cost. The question asks only about NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> from the spiral.

q: In the first step of glycolysis, glucose + ATP → glucose 6-phosphate + ADP. Which enzyme class catalyzes this step?
h: A phosphate group is moved from ATP to glucose.
w: Moving a phosphate group from one molecule to another is a group transfer, so hexokinase is a transferase (a kinase).
x: A hydrolase uses water to split a bond. Here a phosphate group is moved from ATP onto glucose.
An isomerase rearranges atoms within one molecule. This step moves a group between two molecules.
A lyase adds or removes groups to form or break double bonds, or splits a molecule without water. Here a phosphate is passed from ATP to glucose.

q: Where in the cell does glycolysis take place?
h: Glycolysis does not need mitochondria at all.
w: Glycolysis runs in the cytosol. The citric acid cycle is in the mitochondrial matrix, and the electron transport chain is in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
x: The mitochondrial matrix is where the citric acid cycle and β-oxidation run. Glycolysis does not need mitochondria.
The inner mitochondrial membrane holds the electron transport chain. Glycolysis happens before anything enters the mitochondria.
The nucleus stores DNA and makes RNA. Energy pathways like glycolysis are not run there.

q: Which step of glycolysis is an isomerization (atoms rearranged within one molecule)?
h: Look for a step where the formula stays the same and only the arrangement changes.
w: Glucose 6-phosphate (an aldose) is rearranged into fructose 6-phosphate (a ketose) with the same formula, so the enzyme is an isomerase. Splitting into two sugars is a lyase step, and the G3P step is an oxidation.
x: Splitting one six-carbon sugar into two three-carbon sugars is a cleavage (lyase) step. An isomerization keeps one molecule with the same formula.
This step is an oxidation: NAD<sup>+</sup> is reduced and a phosphate is added, so the formula changes.
This step transfers a phosphate from phosphoenolpyruvate to ADP, making ATP. The formula changes, so it is not an isomerization.

q: Which two steps of glycolysis use ATP?
h: ATP is invested early, in the six-carbon half of the pathway.
w: The two phosphorylations of the six-carbon sugar use ATP: glucose → glucose 6-phosphate and fructose 6-phosphate → fructose 1,6-bisphosphate. The two later steps listed in the second choice make ATP.
x: Both of these steps make ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. ATP is spent earlier, in the six-carbon half of the pathway.
The first step uses ATP, but phosphoenolpyruvate → pyruvate makes ATP. Look for the other phosphorylation of a six-carbon sugar.
Neither of these steps uses ATP. The G3P step uses NAD<sup>+</sup> and inorganic phosphate, and the other is a rearrangement and dehydration.

q: Salivary amylase begins the digestion of which carbohydrate in the mouth?
h: Amylase breaks α(1→4) glycosidic bonds in a plant polysaccharide.
w: Amylase hydrolyzes the α(1→4) bonds of starch. Humans have no enzyme for the β(1→4) bonds of cellulose, and the disaccharides lactose and sucrose are broken down by lactase and sucrase in the small intestine.
x: Cellulose has β(1→4) bonds, and humans have no enzyme that breaks them. Amylase works on α(1→4) bonds.
Lactose is a disaccharide broken down by lactase in the small intestine, not by salivary amylase.
Sucrose is a disaccharide broken down by sucrase in the small intestine. Amylase acts on a plant polysaccharide.

q: When oxygen is low, muscle cells reduce pyruvate to lactate. What is the main purpose of this reaction?
c: to regenerate NAD<sup>+</sup> so glycolysis can continue
to make extra ATP from pyruvate
to convert pyruvate back into glucose
h: Glycolysis needs a steady supply of an oxidized coenzyme.
w: Reducing pyruvate oxidizes NADH back to NAD+, which the glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate step of glycolysis needs. The lactate step itself makes no ATP and releases no CO2.
x: Turning pyruvate into lactate makes no ATP itself. Think about which coenzyme gets recycled so glycolysis can keep going.
Pyruvate and lactate both have three carbons, so no CO<sub>2</sub> is released.
Converting lactate back to glucose happens later in the liver (gluconeogenesis). In the muscle, this step serves glycolysis.

q: What are the products of alcoholic fermentation of pyruvate in yeast?
h: Bread rises and beer bubbles because of a gas.
w: Yeast decarboxylates pyruvate to acetaldehyde (releasing CO2) and then reduces it to ethanol, regenerating NAD+. Acetyl CoA is the aerobic route, and lactate is made by muscle and some bacteria.
x: Lactate is what muscle (and some bacteria) make. Yeast makes a product that leaves bubbles in bread and beer.
Acetyl CoA and CO<sub>2</sub> come from the aerobic route (pyruvate dehydrogenase). Fermentation happens without O<sub>2</sub> and makes a different product.
Fermentation does not produce O<sub>2</sub>; it happens when O<sub>2</sub> is lacking. The gas released has a carbon in it.

q: Which hormone stimulates the liver to break glycogen down to glucose when blood glucose is low?
h: This hormone comes from the pancreas and works opposite to insulin.
w: Glucagon (and epinephrine) trigger glycogenolysis in the liver to raise blood glucose. Insulin does the opposite: it promotes glycogen synthesis.
x: Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting glycogen synthesis. You need the hormone that works the opposite way.
Aldosterone controls sodium and water balance in the kidney. It does not trigger glycogen breakdown.
Oxytocin is involved in childbirth and milk release. It does not regulate blood glucose.

q: Glycogen is highly branched. Which glycosidic bond forms its branch points?
h: The straight chains use one link; the branches use carbon 6.
w: Glycogen chains are joined by α(1→4) bonds, and the branches attach through α(1→6) bonds, about every 8–12 glucose units.
x: α(1→4) bonds join the glucose units in the straight chains. Branches attach through a different carbon.
β(1→4) bonds are found in cellulose, not glycogen. Glycogen uses only α bonds.
Glycogen does not use β bonds. Its branch points are α linkages.

q: In the Cori cycle, lactate made by working muscle travels in the blood to which organ, where it is converted back to glucose?
h: This organ is the main site of gluconeogenesis.
w: Lactate goes to the liver, which makes glucose from it by gluconeogenesis and sends the glucose back to the muscle.
x: The brain uses glucose but cannot make it from lactate. Lactate goes to the main site of gluconeogenesis.
The kidney can do some gluconeogenesis, but the Cori cycle is defined by one main organ that returns glucose to muscle.
Adipose tissue stores fat. It does not convert lactate back into glucose.

q: What are the two main products of the pentose phosphate pathway?
h: One product is used for biosynthesis and protection against oxidation; the other is used to build nucleotides.
w: The pathway makes NADPH (for fatty acid synthesis and for keeping glutathione reduced) and ribose 5-phosphate (for nucleotides such as those in DNA, RNA and ATP).
x: NADH and ATP come from glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. The pentose phosphate pathway makes a different reduced coenzyme and a five-carbon sugar.
Pyruvate and lactate come from glycolysis and fermentation. This pathway makes a sugar used for nucleotides.
Acetyl CoA and FADH<sub>2</sub> come from pyruvate oxidation, β-oxidation and the citric acid cycle, not from this pathway.

q: Gluconeogenesis makes new glucose from noncarbohydrate sources. Which of these can NOT be used as a starting material?
c: fatty acids with an even number of carbons
h: Think about whether the carbon atoms can end up in pyruvate or oxaloacetate.
w: Even-chain fatty acids break down to acetyl CoA, and humans cannot convert acetyl CoA into glucose. Lactate, glycerol (from triacylglycerols) and glucogenic amino acids such as alanine can all be used.
x: Lactate can be oxidized back to pyruvate, so it is a good starting material for new glucose (as in the Cori cycle).
Glycerol from triacylglycerols becomes a triose phosphate, so it can be used to make glucose.
Alanine is transaminated to pyruvate, so its carbons can be used to make glucose.

q: In glycolysis, the 6-carbon chain is split into two 3-carbon pieces when
h: Look for the step that turns one molecule into two.
w: Aldolase splits fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate.
x: Hexokinase adds a phosphate to glucose; the molecule still has six carbons afterward.
Pyruvate kinase acts at the very end of glycolysis, on a three-carbon molecule. The split has already happened.
Glucose enters the cell intact as a six-carbon molecule. Look for the enzyme step that turns one molecule into two.

q: Phosphofructokinase, the main control point of glycolysis, is slowed down when
c: ATP is plentiful in the cell
blood glucose is low and the muscle is working hard
h: Why would a cell full of energy keep breaking down glucose?
w: High ATP inhibits phosphofructokinase (feedback inhibition); high AMP, a sign of low energy, activates it.
x: High AMP means the cell is low on energy, so it activates phosphofructokinase rather than slowing it.
When the cell needs energy, glycolysis speeds up. Phosphofructokinase slows when energy is already abundant.
A hard-working muscle needs more ATP, so glycolysis speeds up. Think of the signal that the cell already has enough energy.

q: Hexokinase transfers a phosphate group from ATP to glucose. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: What does a kinase move from one molecule to another?
w: A kinase moves a phosphate group from ATP to a substrate, so it is a transferase.
x: A hydrolase uses water to split a bond. Hexokinase moves a phosphate group from ATP onto glucose.
An isomerase rearranges atoms within one molecule. Hexokinase moves a group from one molecule to another.
A lyase adds or removes groups to form or break double bonds without water. Hexokinase moves a phosphate group between molecules.

q: In the liver, fructose from fruit and table sugar enters glycolysis after it is converted to
h: Fructose is split earlier than glucose.
w: Fructose is phosphorylated and split into triose phosphates (dihydroxyacetone phosphate, plus glyceraldehyde that is then phosphorylated to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate), which join glycolysis in its second half.
x: Glycogen is a storage polymer. Fructose enters the glycolysis pathway itself, not the storage route.
Fructose does not skip all the way to pyruvate. It joins glycolysis partway through, after being split.
Galactose is a different sugar from milk. Fructose is not converted to galactose before entering glycolysis.

q: A newborn with galactosemia cannot convert galactose into a glucose derivative. Which diet change is required?
c: remove lactose (milk sugar) from the diet
h: Which disaccharide releases galactose when it is digested?
w: Lactose = glucose + galactose, so infants with galactosemia need a lactose-free (galactose-free) formula, and milk sugar is avoided for life.
x: Starch is made only of glucose units, so it does not supply galactose.
Protein supplies amino acids, not galactose. The problem is a sugar these infants cannot process.
Adding galactose would make things worse: these infants cannot convert it, so it builds up to toxic levels.

q: Insulin released after a meal stimulates the liver to
h: Insulin is the hormone of the fed state: store or release?
w: Insulin promotes storage: it activates glycogen synthase, so the liver carries out glycogenesis.
x: Glycogen breakdown releases glucose when blood glucose is low. Insulin is the fed-state hormone that promotes storage.
Making new glucose happens during fasting, under glucagon. Insulin signals that glucose is plentiful.
Releasing glucose into the blood raises blood glucose. Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting storage.

q: Why does the brain suffer quickly when blood glucose falls too low?
c: it relies mostly on glucose as its fuel and stores very little glycogen
it stores large amounts of glucose that become toxic
it makes its own glucose by gluconeogenesis
h: Think about the brain’s fuel supply and its reserves.
w: Under normal conditions the brain burns glucose almost exclusively and has very little glycogen, so hypoglycemia quickly causes confusion and loss of consciousness.
x: The brain stores very little glucose or glycogen. Its problem is having almost no reserve.
The brain uses a lot of oxygen; it relies on aerobic metabolism of its fuel.
Gluconeogenesis happens mainly in the liver (and some in the kidney), not in the brain. The brain depends on glucose delivered by the blood.

q: In the last step of glycolysis, pyruvate kinase transfers a phosphate from phosphoenolpyruvate directly to ADP. This way of making ATP is called
c: phosphorylation driven by a proton pump
h: Does this step use the electron transport chain?
w: The phosphate goes straight from a substrate to ADP: substrate-level phosphorylation.
x: Proton-pump-driven ATP synthesis is oxidative phosphorylation by ATP synthase. Here the phosphate moves straight from one molecule to ADP.
Photophosphorylation uses light energy in plants. No light is involved in glycolysis.
Dephosphorylation means removing a phosphate. The question asks about the way ADP gains a phosphate to make ATP.

q: Lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to lactate using NADH. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: A dehydrogenase moves hydrogen (electrons) between molecules.
w: Pyruvate is reduced while NADH is oxidized, so lactate dehydrogenase is an oxidoreductase.
x: A transferase moves a functional group, such as a phosphate, between molecules. Here hydrogen (electrons) moves from NADH to pyruvate.
A hydrolase uses water to split a bond. No water is used in converting pyruvate to lactate.
A ligase joins two molecules into one larger molecule. Pyruvate and lactate both have three carbons.

q: A patient with long-term heavy alcohol use is low in thiamine (vitamin B<sub>1</sub>). Thiamine is made into TPP, a coenzyme for decarboxylation (removing CO<sub>2</sub>). Which reaction is impaired, causing lactate to build up?
h: Find the step that removes CO<sub>2</sub> from pyruvate. If pyruvate can’t go forward, what is it reduced to instead?
w: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a coenzyme of pyruvate dehydrogenase, which removes CO2 from pyruvate as it forms acetyl CoA. When that step is blocked, pyruvate is reduced to lactate instead. That is why thiamine is given before or with IV glucose in at-risk patients: a glucose load increases the demand for thiamine.
x: Phosphorylation of glucose uses ATP and hexokinase, not a decarboxylation coenzyme. No CO<sub>2</sub> is removed.
Glycogen breakdown uses phosphate to split glucose units off. It does not remove CO<sub>2</sub>.
Lactate → pyruvate is an oxidation that does not remove CO<sub>2</sub>. Find the step where pyruvate loses a carbon.

q: During a “fight or flight” response, epinephrine raises blood glucose mainly by
c: stimulating glycogen breakdown in liver and muscle
h: Epinephrine prepares the body for action: fuel must be released fast.
w: Epinephrine triggers glycogenolysis (glycogen → glucose 1-phosphate) in liver and muscle.
x: Glycogen synthesis lowers blood glucose by storing it. Epinephrine needs to release fuel quickly.
The brain needs glucose during an emergency; epinephrine does not block its glycolysis.
Insulin lowers blood glucose, the opposite of what epinephrine does.

q: Gluconeogenesis is not simply glycolysis run in reverse because
c: three steps of glycolysis are irreversible and need different enzymes to bypass them
it takes place in the nucleus
it produces pyruvate instead of glucose
h: Some glycolysis steps release so much energy that they cannot run backward.
w: The hexokinase, phosphofructokinase and pyruvate kinase steps are irreversible; gluconeogenesis uses different enzymes to get around each of them.
x: Gluconeogenesis occurs mainly in the cytosol and mitochondria of liver cells, not in the nucleus.
Gluconeogenesis actually costs ATP (and GTP). Making glucose is an energy-requiring, anabolic process.
Gluconeogenesis makes glucose, often starting from pyruvate. Producing pyruvate is what glycolysis does.

q: Glycogen phosphorylase breaks glycogen down by adding phosphate across a glycosidic bond. What is the product released?
h: The phosphate ends up on the carbon that was in the glycosidic bond.
w: Phosphorolysis releases glucose 1-phosphate, which is then isomerized to glucose 6-phosphate.
x: Free glucose would come from adding water (hydrolysis). Phosphorylase adds phosphate across the bond instead.
Glucose 6-phosphate is formed in a later step by isomerization. The phosphate first ends up on the carbon that was in the glycosidic bond.
Glycogen is made only of glucose units, so breaking it down cannot release fructose.

q: In glycogenesis, glucose units are added to the growing glycogen chain from
h: Glucose is first “activated” by attaching it to a nucleotide.
w: Glucose 1-phosphate reacts with UTP to make UDP-glucose, the activated donor that glycogen synthase uses.
x: Free glucose is not reactive enough to be added to glycogen. It must first be activated by attaching it to a nucleotide.
Glucose 6-phosphate is an early intermediate, but it is not the direct donor. It is changed and then attached to a nucleotide.
Lactose is milk sugar (glucose + galactose). It is not used to build glycogen.

q: People with G6PD deficiency can develop hemolytic anemia after eating fava beans or taking certain drugs. Which product of the pentose phosphate pathway is too low in their red blood cells?
h: G6PD is the first enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway.
w: Red blood cells depend on the pentose phosphate pathway for NADPH, which protects them from oxidative damage.
x: Red blood cells make their ATP by glycolysis, not by the pentose phosphate pathway. Think of the product that protects against oxidation.
Lactate is made by glycolysis in red blood cells. It is not a pentose phosphate pathway product.
Glycogen is a storage polymer and not a product of the pentose phosphate pathway.

q: Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon, epinephrine and cortisol raise it by turning on glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis in the liver. After surgery or a serious illness, blood glucose often rises even in people without diabetes. This “stress hyperglycemia” is caused mainly by
c: release of epinephrine and cortisol in response to physical stress
extra insulin release from the pancreas
increased glycogen synthesis in the liver
h: Which hormones prepare the body for an emergency?
w: Cortisol and epinephrine (with glucagon) raise blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis: stress hormones.
x: Extra insulin would lower blood glucose, not raise it. Think about hormones released in an emergency.
Glycogen synthesis removes glucose from the blood. Stress hyperglycemia involves glucose being released.
Less glucagon would lower blood glucose. Glucagon is one of the hormones that raises it.

q: Humans cannot digest cellulose because
c: we have no enzyme that hydrolyzes its β(1→4) glycosidic bonds
h: Starch and cellulose are both glucose polymers. What is different?
w: Our amylases break α(1→4) bonds only; cellulose has β(1→4) bonds, so it passes through as dietary fiber.
x: Cellulose is made of glucose, just like starch. The difference is in how the glucose units are linked.
Cellulose is a polysaccharide (a carbohydrate), not a protein.
Stomach acid does not break down cellulose; it passes through the gut intact as fiber. Think about which enzymes we lack.

q: A person with lactose intolerance drinks milk and develops bloating and diarrhea. Why?
c: low lactase lets undigested lactose reach the colon, where bacteria ferment it
milk protein is digested too fast
h: Which enzyme splits lactose, and where does undigested lactose end up?
w: Without enough brush-border lactase, lactose reaches the colon; bacteria ferment it to gas and acids, and water follows the sugar.
x: The problem is that lactose is not absorbed at all. Undigested lactose travels on into the large intestine.
Milk protein digestion is not the issue here. The symptoms come from the milk sugar.
Liver glycogen storage is not involved. The problem is in the gut, with a missing digestive enzyme.

q: After about a day without food, liver glycogen is nearly used up. What then becomes the main source of blood glucose?
h: Muscle glycogen cannot leave the muscle as glucose.
w: When liver glycogen runs out, the liver makes new glucose from lactate, glycerol and amino acids by gluconeogenesis.
x: Muscle glycogen fuels the muscle itself; muscle lacks the enzyme to release free glucose into the blood.
After a day without food, there is no dietary starch to digest. Blood glucose must come from inside the body.
The pentose phosphate pathway makes NADPH and ribose 5-phosphate. It uses glucose rather than producing it.

q: Glycerol released when stored fat is broken down can be used to make glucose. It enters the glycolysis/gluconeogenesis pathway as
h: Glycerol has three carbons; which three-carbon intermediate does it resemble?
w: Glycerol is phosphorylated and oxidized to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, a triose phosphate of glycolysis.
x: Glycerol enters higher up than pyruvate. It joins as a three-carbon sugar phosphate, the same kind formed when fructose 1,6-bisphosphate splits.
Acetyl CoA cannot be turned into glucose in humans. Glycerol can, because it enters at a different point.
Lactate is formed from pyruvate in muscle. Glycerol is phosphorylated and oxidized to a triose phosphate instead.

q: Citrate synthase catalyzes the first step of the citric acid cycle: acetyl CoA + oxaloacetate → citrate + CoA–SH. Which enzyme class is it?
h: Follow the acetyl group, and ask whether ATP is spent.
w: Citrate synthase moves the acetyl group from acetyl CoA onto oxaloacetate, and CoA–SH leaves, so it is a transferase. No ATP is spent (the thioester bond of acetyl CoA supplies the energy), so it is not a ligase. No water splits a bond (not a hydrolase), and no hydrogen is removed (not an oxidoreductase).
x: A ligase spends ATP to join two molecules. Citrate synthase spends no ATP; it transfers the acetyl group of acetyl CoA onto oxaloacetate.
A hydrolase splits a bond using water. Here an acetyl group is moved onto oxaloacetate to make a larger molecule.
An oxidoreductase moves electrons (hydrogen). No hydrogen is removed when citrate is formed here.

q: How many molecules of CO<sub>2</sub> are released in one turn of the citric acid cycle?
h: Two carbons come in as acetyl CoA each turn.
w: Two carbons enter as acetyl CoA and two CO2 leave (at the isocitrate and α-ketoglutarate steps).
x: Two carbons come in as acetyl CoA each turn, and the cycle releases the same number of carbons as CO<sub>2</sub>.
Three CO<sub>2</sub> would include the carbon lost when pyruvate becomes acetyl CoA, which happens before the cycle.
Six CO<sub>2</sub> is the total for a whole glucose molecule. One turn of the cycle handles only one acetyl group.

q: Where in the mitochondrion are the complexes of the electron transport chain located?
h: The chain must build a proton gradient across a membrane.
w: The complexes are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane (the cristae).
x: The outer membrane is leaky and cannot hold a proton gradient. The complexes sit in the membrane that encloses the matrix.
The complexes are not floating free; they must be embedded in a membrane to pump H<sup>+</sup> across it.
The cytosol is outside the mitochondrion, where glycolysis happens. The chain is part of the mitochondrion.

q: During electron transport, H<sup>+</sup> ions are pumped
c: from the matrix into the intermembrane space, then flow back through ATP synthase
from the cytosol into the nucleus
into the matrix, then out through complex I
h: ATP synthase lets the protons return. Where do they return to?
w: The complexes pump H+ into the intermembrane space; the protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, which makes ATP (chemiosmosis).
x: The nucleus is not involved in electron transport. The H<sup>+</sup> pumping happens across a mitochondrial membrane.
Protons are not pumped out of the cell. They are moved across a membrane inside the mitochondrion.
This is backward: complex I pumps H<sup>+</sup> out of the matrix. Protons flow back in through ATP synthase.

q: Besides binding hemoglobin, carbon monoxide (like cyanide) can also bind cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), the last complex of the electron transport chain, where electrons are passed to O<sub>2</sub>. What happens in a cell where complex IV is blocked?
c: electrons cannot reach O<sub>2</sub>, so the H<sup>+</sup> gradient and ATP synthesis stop
ATP synthase makes ATP faster to compensate
glucose is oxidized directly to CO<sub>2</sub> without NADH
the citric acid cycle speeds up because NAD<sup>+</sup> builds up
h: If the last carrier is blocked, can electrons keep flowing? What powers ATP synthase?
w: With complex IV blocked, electrons back up and can’t reach O2. Proton pumping stops, the H+ gradient collapses, and ATP synthesis stops. NADH can’t be reoxidized, so the citric acid cycle slows too (it does not speed up).
x: ATP synthase is powered by the H<sup>+</sup> gradient. If electron flow stops, the gradient is not maintained, so it cannot speed up.
Glucose still needs NADH-producing pathways to be oxidized to CO<sub>2</sub>. A blocked chain cannot change that.
With complex IV blocked, NADH cannot be reoxidized, so NAD<sup>+</sup> runs short rather than building up.

q: Oxidative phosphorylation means that ATP is made
c: by ATP synthase, using energy from electron transport
by transferring phosphate from a substrate to ADP
h: Which process links oxidation (electron transport) to phosphorylation?
w: Energy released as electrons pass along the chain builds a proton gradient that drives ATP synthase: oxidative phosphorylation.
x: Transferring phosphate from a substrate to ADP is substrate-level phosphorylation, as in glycolysis.
Breaking down glycogen releases glucose (as glucose 1-phosphate). It does not describe how ATP is made.
Hydrolyzing ATP uses ATP up, releasing energy. Oxidative phosphorylation is about making ATP.

q: The citric acid cycle does not use O<sub>2</sub> directly, yet it stops when O<sub>2</sub> runs out. Why?
c: NAD<sup>+</sup> and FAD are no longer regenerated by electron transport
O<sub>2</sub> is a substrate of citrate synthase
CO<sub>2</sub> builds up in the matrix
h: Where does the cycle get its oxidized coenzymes?
w: The cycle needs NAD<sup>+</sup> and FAD; without O<sub>2</sub> the electron transport chain cannot reoxidize NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub>, so the cycle stops.
x: Citrate synthase joins acetyl CoA and oxaloacetate; O<sub>2</sub> is not one of its substrates.
CO<sub>2</sub> diffuses out readily and is not what stops the cycle. Think about the coenzymes the cycle needs.
ATP synthase running backward is not the reason. The cycle depends on oxidized coenzymes being recycled.

q: Complete oxidation of glucose gives about 32 ATP in liver cells but about 30 ATP in muscle and brain cells. Why?
c: the two cytosolic NADH from glycolysis enter the electron transport chain by different shuttles
brain cells lack the citric acid cycle
liver mitochondria have more ATP synthase per NADH
h: Cytosolic NADH cannot cross the inner membrane itself.
w: In liver and heart the malate–aspartate shuttle delivers the electrons as NADH (2.5 ATP each); in muscle and brain the glycerol-phosphate shuttle delivers them as FADH<sub>2</sub> (1.5 ATP each).
x: Muscle and liver both make 2 pyruvate per glucose. The difference involves the cytosolic NADH from glycolysis.
Brain cells do have a working citric acid cycle; they rely on aerobic metabolism of glucose.
Each NADH that enters the chain gives the same ATP in any cell. The difference is in how cytosolic NADH electrons get into the mitochondria.

q: NAD<sup>+</sup>, which carries electrons to the electron transport chain, is made from which vitamin?
h: NAD stands for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide.
w: Nicotinamide comes from niacin; FAD comes from riboflavin.
x: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) is used to make FAD, the other electron carrier.
Vitamin C is an antioxidant needed for collagen synthesis. It is not part of NAD<sup>+</sup>.
Vitamin K is needed for blood clotting. It is not used to make NAD<sup>+</sup>.

q: Fat provides about 9 kcal g⁻¹ but carbohydrate only about 4 kcal g⁻¹. Why?
c: the carbons of fat are more reduced (more C–H, fewer C–O bonds), so their oxidation yields more NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub>
carbohydrates are not oxidized by the citric acid cycle
h: Which is already partly oxidized: a carbon with an –OH, or a CH<sub>2</sub>?
w: Carbohydrate carbons already carry oxygen; fat carbons are mostly CH<sub>2</sub>, so each has more electrons to give to NAD<sup>+</sup> and FAD.
x: Fats (triacylglycerols) contain only C, H and O; they have no nitrogen.
Carbohydrates are oxidized through glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. The difference is how oxidized their carbons already are.
Size is not the reason. A triacylglycerol is actually a fairly large molecule; compare the C–H and C–O bonds per carbon.

q: As electrons move along the electron transport chain, most of the energy they release is first stored as
c: a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) gradient across the inner membrane
h: ATP synthase is powered by something the chain builds.
w: The energy is captured as a proton gradient; ATP synthase then converts part of it into ATP and the rest is released as heat.
x: Glycogen is a stored carbohydrate. The energy from electron transport is stored across a membrane.
Some energy is lost as heat, but most is first captured in a form that powers ATP synthase.
NADH is the electron donor at the start of the chain. The energy released along the chain is stored in another form.

q: Why are the brain and heart damaged within minutes when their oxygen supply stops?
c: they depend on oxidative phosphorylation for most of their ATP and have little stored energy
they make ATP only by glycolysis
oxygen is a structural part of their proteins
they cannot carry out the citric acid cycle
h: Compare the ATP yield of glycolysis alone with complete oxidation.
w: Without O2, electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation stop and ATP output falls to the small yield of glycolysis.
x: These organs make most of their ATP aerobically. Glycolysis alone gives only a small amount of ATP.
Oxygen is needed as the final electron acceptor, not as a building block of proteins.
The brain and heart do carry out the citric acid cycle. The problem is what happens to ATP output when O<sub>2</sub> is missing.

q: Put the stages of complete glucose oxidation in order.
c: glycolysis → pyruvate oxidation → citric acid cycle → electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation
citric acid cycle → glycolysis → electron transport → pyruvate oxidation
pyruvate oxidation → glycolysis → electron transport → citric acid cycle
electron transport → citric acid cycle → glycolysis → pyruvate oxidation
h: Glucose is split first, in the cytosol.
w: Glucose → pyruvate (glycolysis) → acetyl CoA (pyruvate oxidation) → citric acid cycle → NADH and FADH2 used by electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation.
x: The citric acid cycle needs acetyl CoA, which comes from glucose first being split and pyruvate oxidized.
Pyruvate oxidation needs pyruvate, which only exists after glucose is split. Glucose is broken down first, in the cytosol.
The electron transport chain needs NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> from earlier stages, so it cannot come first.

q: Where in the cell does β-oxidation take place?
h: The fatty acid is carried across the inner mitochondrial membrane first.
w: After the carnitine shuttle, β-oxidation runs in the mitochondrial matrix, next to the citric acid cycle.
x: The cytosol is where fatty acids are made (lipogenesis). Breakdown happens after the carnitine shuttle moves them across a membrane.
The nucleus holds DNA and does not break down fatty acids.
The endoplasmic reticulum is involved in lipid synthesis, not β-oxidation. The fatty acid is carried into another organelle.

q: During fasting, glucagon and epinephrine activate hormone-sensitive lipase in fat cells. What does it release into the blood?
c: fatty acids and glycerol from stored triacylglycerols
h: A lipase hydrolyzes ester bonds in fats.
w: Hormone-sensitive lipase hydrolyzes stored triacylglycerols into fatty acids and glycerol, which travel to other tissues.
x: Glycogen breakdown is done by glycogen phosphorylase, mainly in liver and muscle. A lipase acts on fats.
Muscle protein breakdown uses proteases, not lipases. A lipase hydrolyzes ester bonds in fats.
Ketone bodies are made in the liver from acetyl CoA, not released directly from fat cells.

q: Lipoproteins carry cholesterol and triacylglycerols in the blood. Which statement about LDL and HDL is correct?
c: LDL carries cholesterol to the tissues; HDL carries cholesterol back to the liver
HDL carries dietary fat from the intestine
LDL is protective and HDL is harmful
h: Which one is called “good” cholesterol, and why?
w: LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues (high levels linked to plaque); HDL returns excess cholesterol to the liver.
x: Dietary fat leaves the intestine in chylomicrons, not HDL. HDL is involved in moving cholesterol.
This is backward. High LDL is linked to plaque, while HDL is called "good" cholesterol.
Lipoproteins carry lipids such as cholesterol and triacylglycerols. Glucose dissolves in blood and needs no lipoprotein.

q: After a fatty meal, dietary triacylglycerols leave the intestine packed in which lipoprotein?
h: This is the largest, least dense lipoprotein.
w: Intestinal cells package absorbed fat into chylomicrons, which enter the lymph and then the blood.
x: LDL carries cholesterol to tissues. It is formed in the blood from lipoproteins made by the liver, not from the intestine.
HDL collects cholesterol and returns it to the liver. It does not carry newly absorbed dietary fat.
Albumin carries free fatty acids in the blood, but it is not a lipoprotein and does not package triacylglycerols.

q: Which of these is NOT a ketone body?
h: Ketone bodies are made from acetyl CoA in the liver.
w: The three ketone bodies are acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate and acetone. Pyruvate is the product of glycolysis.
x: Acetoacetate is a ketone body made from acetyl CoA in the liver.
β-Hydroxybutyrate is a ketone body formed by reducing acetoacetate.
Acetone is a ketone body; it gives the fruity breath smell in ketosis.

q: The liver makes ketone bodies during fasting, but it does not use them. Which tissues use them for energy?
c: heart, muscle and (after several days) the brain
no tissue; they are only excreted
h: Ketone bodies are fuel sent out from the liver.
w: Ketone bodies are exported to heart, skeletal muscle and the brain (once it adapts); the liver lacks the enzyme needed to use them.
x: The liver makes ketone bodies but lacks the enzyme needed to use them. They are exported as fuel.
Red blood cells have no mitochondria, so they cannot use ketone bodies. They rely on glycolysis.
Some ketone bodies are lost in urine and breath, but most are used as fuel by other tissues.

q: Fatty acid synthesis (lipogenesis) adds carbons to the growing chain two at a time from
c: malonyl CoA (as malonyl ACP), releasing CO<sub>2</sub>
h: A three-carbon unit is added and one carbon leaves as CO<sub>2</sub>.
w: Each turn adds a two-carbon unit from malonyl ACP; its third carbon leaves as CO2.
x: Acetoacetate is a ketone body, not a building block for fatty acid synthesis.
Glycerol forms the backbone of triacylglycerols; it does not add carbons to a fatty acid chain.
Ketone bodies are made during fasting from fat breakdown. They are not used to build fatty acids.

q: Which hormone promotes lipogenesis and fat storage after a carbohydrate-rich meal?
h: Which hormone signals the fed state?
w: Insulin promotes fatty acid synthesis and storage of triacylglycerols; glucagon and epinephrine promote fat breakdown.
x: Glucagon is a fasting hormone; it promotes fat breakdown, not storage.
Epinephrine mobilizes fuel for action, including fat breakdown. It does not promote fat storage.
Cortisol is a stress hormone that raises blood glucose. It is not the main fed-state signal for fat storage.

q: Transamination enzymes (such as ALT and AST) require which coenzyme?
h: The coenzyme carries the amino group between molecules.
w: Every transaminase uses pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) to carry the amino group.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> accepts hydrogen in oxidation reactions. Transaminases move an amino group, not hydrogen.
FAD accepts hydrogen in oxidations such as succinate → fumarate. It does not carry amino groups.
Coenzyme A carries acyl groups like acetyl. Transamination needs a carrier for amino groups.

q: ALT is a transamination enzyme found mainly inside liver cells. A blood test shows a high level of ALT. What is the best explanation?
c: injured liver cells are leaking ALT into the blood
the liver is making extra ALT to speed up transamination
a high-protein meal raised the blood ALT
h: ALT works inside cells. How would it get into the blood?
w: ALT normally stays inside liver cells. When the cells are damaged, their contents leak into the blood, so a high ALT signals liver injury.
x: ALT does its work inside liver cells. A higher level in the blood signals that something let it out.
ALT is normally kept inside cells, so blood levels are not set by kidney excretion. Think about how an enzyme from inside cells reaches the blood.
Eating protein does not release ALT into the blood. Blood ALT rises when liver cells are damaged.

q: In which organ is urea made?
h: Urea is made in one organ and excreted by another.
w: The urea cycle runs in the liver; the kidneys then excrete urea in the urine.
x: The kidneys excrete urea in the urine, but they do not make it.
The pancreas makes digestive enzymes and hormones like insulin, not urea.
Muscle sends nitrogen out (for example as alanine or glutamine), but it does not run the urea cycle.

q: Urea is made in the liver and removed from the blood by the kidneys. A patient with kidney failure has a high blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Why?
c: the kidneys cannot excrete the urea that the liver keeps making
the liver makes too much glucose
the patient is not eating protein
h: Where is urea made, and where does it leave the body?
w: The liver keeps producing urea, but failing kidneys cannot clear it, so urea accumulates in the blood.
x: Glucose production does not affect blood urea. BUN measures urea, the nitrogen waste the kidneys remove.
If the urea cycle stopped, urea would fall and ammonia would rise. In kidney failure, urea is still being made.
Eating less protein would lower urea production, not raise BUN.

q: In severe liver failure, blood ammonia rises and the patient becomes confused (hepatic encephalopathy). Why does ammonia build up?
c: the failing liver cannot convert ammonium ion into urea
the kidneys excrete too much urea
h: Which liver pathway disposes of nitrogen?
w: Ammonium from amino acid breakdown is normally turned into urea in the liver; when the urea cycle fails, ammonia accumulates and is toxic to the brain.
x: In liver failure, less urea is made, not more. And excreting urea would not raise blood ammonia.
Making glucose does not produce ammonia. Think about which liver pathway disposes of nitrogen.
Fatty acids contain no nitrogen, so they cannot release ammonia.

q: Which person is most likely to be in positive nitrogen balance (taking in more nitrogen than is excreted)?
c: a person on a very low-protein diet
h: Positive balance means protein is being built up.
w: Growth, pregnancy and recovery build new protein, so a growing child retains nitrogen: positive nitrogen balance.
x: Fasting breaks down body protein for fuel, so more nitrogen is excreted than eaten: negative balance.
Severe burns cause rapid muscle protein breakdown, which gives a negative nitrogen balance.
Too little protein in the diet means the body breaks down its own protein, so nitrogen balance is negative.

q: A patient with extensive burns breaks down muscle protein faster than it is replaced. What is her nitrogen balance?
c: nitrogen balance does not apply to protein
h: Is she excreting more nitrogen than she takes in?
w: Net protein breakdown means more nitrogen is excreted (as urea) than eaten: negative nitrogen balance.
x: Positive balance means protein is being built up, as in growth or recovery. She is breaking protein down faster than it is replaced.
Zero balance would mean breakdown and replacement are equal. Here breakdown is faster.
Proteins are the body's main nitrogen source, so nitrogen balance is exactly how protein gain or loss is measured.

q: An amino acid whose carbon skeleton is degraded to pyruvate or a citric acid cycle intermediate is called
h: Which of those products can be turned into glucose?
w: Pyruvate and cycle intermediates can be made into glucose, so the amino acid is glucogenic.
x: Ketogenic amino acids are broken down to acetyl CoA or acetoacetate, which cannot be made into glucose.
Essential means the body cannot make the amino acid and it must come from the diet. That says nothing about what its skeleton becomes.
Nonpolar describes the side chain's polarity, not what the carbon skeleton is converted into.

q: In phenylketonuria (PKU), phenylalanine hydroxylase is missing, so phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine. What is the treatment? (Phenylalanine is both glucogenic and ketogenic.)
c: a low-phenylalanine diet, avoiding aspartame, beginning in infancy
h: The goal is to keep phenylalanine from building up.
w: A lifelong low-phenylalanine diet prevents the build-up that damages the developing brain; aspartame contains phenylalanine and carries a warning label.
x: A high-protein diet would add more phenylalanine, which builds up when it cannot be converted to tyrosine.
Extra phenylalanine would make the build-up worse and damage the developing brain.
Carbohydrates are not the problem in PKU. The issue is one amino acid that cannot be processed.

q: Glutamate undergoes oxidative deamination in the liver. Besides NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, what are the products?
h: The amino group leaves and the carbon becomes a C=O; NAD<sup>+</sup> is the oxidizing agent.
w: Glutamate dehydrogenase removes the amino group as NH4+, leaving α-ketoglutarate, and reduces NAD+ to NADH.
x: Pyruvate comes from deaminating alanine, not glutamate. And this step reduces NAD<sup>+</sup>, not FAD.
Aspartate and ATP are not made here. Glutamate loses its amino group, and its carbon skeleton becomes a keto acid.
Urea is made later in the urea cycle, and no carbon is lost as CO<sub>2</sub> in this step.

q: Complete oxidation of stearic acid (18 carbons, saturated) gives 120 ATP. Oleic acid also has 18 carbons but one C=C. In this course, each C=C that is already present skips one FAD step of β-oxidation (1.5 ATP). How many ATP does oleic acid give?
h: Same number of carbons means the same acetyl CoA. Subtract one FADH<sub>2</sub> for the double bond.
w: Oleic acid gives the same 9 acetyl CoA and 8 NADH as stearic acid, but one fewer FADH2 because its C=C is already there. 120 − 1.5 = 118.5 ATP.
x: 120 is the value for saturated stearic acid. The C=C in oleic acid means one FADH<sub>2</sub> is not made.
117.5 subtracts 2.5, the value for NADH. The step that is skipped is the FAD step, worth 1.5 ATP.
An existing double bond lowers the yield; it does not raise it. Less oxidation happens, so less ATP is made.

q: Linoleic acid (18 carbons, two C=C bonds) and stearic acid (18 carbons, saturated) are both oxidized completely. Compared with stearic acid, β-oxidation of linoleic acid produces
c: two fewer FADH<sub>2</sub> but the same number of acetyl CoA (9)
two fewer NADH but the same number of FADH<sub>2</sub>
h: The number of acetyl CoA depends on the number of carbons. Which step does a double bond that is already present skip?
w: Both fatty acids have 18 carbons, so both give 9 acetyl CoA. Each existing C=C skips the FAD step once, so linoleic acid gives two fewer FADH2 and therefore less ATP.
x: Acetyl CoA comes from the carbon chain two carbons at a time. Both acids have 18 carbons.
The step that is skipped is the one that forms a C=C, which uses FAD, not NAD<sup>+</sup>.
The double bonds already present change the count of one reduced coenzyme, so the products are not identical.

q: Fatty acids are activated as fatty acyl CoA at the outer mitochondrial membrane, but β-oxidation happens in the mitochondrial matrix. Which molecule carries the fatty acyl group across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
h: This carrier gives its name to the "shuttle" that moves fatty acyl groups into the mitochondria.
w: Fatty acyl CoA cannot cross the inner membrane. The acyl group is moved onto carnitine, carried across, and then moved back onto CoA inside the matrix (the carnitine shuttle).
x: Coenzyme A carries the acyl group on each side of the membrane, but acyl CoA cannot cross the inner membrane itself.
Albumin carries free fatty acids in the blood, not across the mitochondrial membrane.
Chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the intestine through the lymph and blood. They do not enter mitochondria.

q: Which is NOT a source of amino acids for the body's amino acid pool?
c: fatty acids released from stored fat
breakdown of the body's own proteins (protein turnover)
synthesis of nonessential amino acids in the liver
h: Amino acids contain nitrogen. Which choice has no nitrogen to give?
w: The amino acid pool is fed by dietary protein, by protein turnover, and by synthesis of nonessential amino acids. Fatty acids contain no nitrogen, so they cannot be made into amino acids.
x: Digested dietary protein is the main source of new amino acids for the pool.
Body proteins are constantly broken down, and their amino acids return to the pool.
The liver makes nonessential amino acids, for example by transamination, and adds them to the pool.

q: What does protein turnover mean?
c: Body proteins are continuously broken down and resynthesized
Dietary protein is digested only in the stomach
Proteins are converted into stored fat
Amino acids are excreted unchanged in the urine
h: Turnover is the same idea as staff turnover at a job: the old ones leave and new ones replace them.
w: Protein turnover is the ongoing breakdown of body proteins into amino acids and the building of new proteins from the amino acid pool. It lets cells replace damaged proteins and adjust enzyme levels.
x: Protein digestion starts in the stomach and finishes in the small intestine. Turnover is about the body's own proteins.
Excess amino acids can end up as fat after their nitrogen is removed, but that is not what turnover means.
Healthy kidneys excrete very few free amino acids. Excess nitrogen leaves as urea.

q: The body has no storage form for amino acids. What happens to amino acids in the pool that are not needed for making proteins and other nitrogen compounds?
c: Their amino groups are removed and become urea, and their carbon skeletons are used for energy or made into glucose or fat
They are stored as a reserve protein in muscle, the way glucose is stored as glycogen
They are excreted unchanged in the urine
They are converted into essential amino acids
h: Think about transamination, deamination and the urea cycle.
w: Extra amino acids are not stored. Their nitrogen is removed (transamination and oxidative deamination) and excreted as urea, and the carbon skeletons enter pathways that give energy, glucose or fat.
x: Muscle proteins all have jobs to do; there is no storage protein comparable to glycogen.
Healthy kidneys do not excrete amino acids. The nitrogen leaves as urea.
The body cannot make the carbon skeletons of essential amino acids, so extra amino acids cannot be turned into them.

q: A clinic patient has a fasting blood glucose of 132 mg/dL and an A1C of 7.1%. Using the usual cut-offs (fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or higher, or A1C 6.5% or higher), how should these results be read?
h: Compare each result with its cut-off.
w: A fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher and an A1C of 6.5% or higher are both in the diabetes range, and this patient is above both (132 mg/dL and 7.1%).
x: Normal fasting glucose is 99 mg/dL or lower, and normal A1C is below 5.7%. Both results are higher.
Prediabetes is a fasting glucose of 100–125 mg/dL. 132 mg/dL is above that range.
Hypoglycemia means glucose is too low. These values are high.

q: The three ketone bodies are acetoacetate, CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>–COO<sup>−</sup>, β-hydroxybutyrate, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)–CH<sub>2</sub>–COO<sup>−</sup>, and acetone, CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>3</sub>. Which statement about their functional groups is correct?
c: β-Hydroxybutyrate has a hydroxyl group and a carboxylate group but no ketone group.
Acetone has a carboxylic acid group as well as a ketone group.
Acetoacetate has a hydroxyl group and a carboxylate group but no ketone group.
All three have a ketone C=O between two carbons, which is why they are called ketone bodies.
h: A ketone is a C=O with a carbon on each side. Check each formula for that group, for –OH and for –COO<sup>−</sup>.
w: β-Hydroxybutyrate has an –OH on its β carbon where acetoacetate has a C=O, so it is a "ketone body" that is not a ketone. Acetoacetate is a ketone and a carboxylate; acetone is only a ketone.
x: Acetone is CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>3</sub>: a ketone and nothing else. With no –COOH group, it is the one ketone body that is not an acid.
That describes β-hydroxybutyrate. Acetoacetate keeps the ketone C=O on its β carbon; reducing that C=O is what makes the hydroxyl compound.
The name is traditional, not exact. β-Hydroxybutyrate has an alcohol carbon, CH(OH), where the ketone carbon would be.

q: During a long fast, why does the liver turn much of its acetyl CoA into ketone bodies instead of oxidizing it in the citric acid cycle?
c: Oxaloacetate is being used to make glucose, so the cycle cannot accept all the acetyl CoA from β-oxidation.
Oxaloacetate builds up and blocks the cycle, so the acetyl CoA from glycolysis has nowhere to go.
The liver has no mitochondria, so it cannot run the citric acid cycle at all.
Insulin is high during a fast, and insulin switches on ketone body formation.
h: Acetyl CoA enters the citric acid cycle by joining a four-carbon acceptor. What else is the liver using that acceptor for when no carbohydrate is coming in?
w: In a fast, fatty acid oxidation floods the liver with acetyl CoA while oxaloacetate is diverted to glucose synthesis. With too little oxaloacetate to accept it, the extra acetyl CoA is joined into acetoacetate, which gives β-hydroxybutyrate and acetone.
x: It is the other way around: oxaloacetate runs low because it is pulled out for glucose synthesis. In a fast the acetyl CoA also comes mainly from fatty acids, not from glycolysis.
Liver cells have many mitochondria, and both β-oxidation and ketone body formation take place there. The cycle still runs; it is just short of oxaloacetate.
Insulin is low during a fast. Low insulin lets fat cells release fatty acids, and that is the source of the extra acetyl CoA.

q: How does ketoacidosis differ from ketosis?
c: In ketosis ketone bodies build up in the blood and urine; in ketoacidosis they overwhelm the blood buffers and blood pH falls.
In ketosis blood pH falls; in ketoacidosis the blood buffers hold the pH at its normal value.
In ketosis only acetone is made; in ketoacidosis the liver makes glucose instead of ketone bodies.
In ketosis blood pH falls below 7.4; in ketoacidosis blood pH rises above 7.4.
h: Both words begin with keto-. What does the extra part, "acidosis", say about the blood?
w: Ketosis means ketone bodies are accumulating in the blood and urine while the pH is still buffered. When the acidic ketone bodies exceed what the buffers can handle, blood pH drops (to 7.30 or lower in DKA), and the condition is ketoacidosis.
x: This reverses the two terms. The word "acidosis" marks the condition in which the pH has actually dropped.
All three ketone bodies are made in both conditions, and the liver is making glucose in both. The difference is whether blood pH has fallen.
Acidosis means the blood has become more acidic, so the pH goes down, not up. In ketosis alone the buffers are still holding the pH.

q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis has fruity-smelling breath. Which ketone body causes the odor, and does it lower blood pH?
c: acetone; it is volatile and is breathed out, and with no carboxylic acid group it does not release H<sup>+</sup>
acetone; it is breathed out, and it is the strongest acid of the three ketone bodies
acetoacetate; it is a volatile acid that is breathed out and also releases H<sup>+</sup>
β-hydroxybutyrate; its –OH group makes it evaporate easily, and it does not release H<sup>+</sup>
h: One ketone body is a small molecule with only a ketone group. Think about which functional group releases H<sup>+</sup> and which molecule evaporates most easily.
w: Acetone, CH3–CO–CH3, is small and volatile, so it leaves the blood in the lungs and is smelled on the breath. It has no carboxylic acid group, so the drop in pH comes from the other two, acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate.
x: Acetone is the right compound, but it is not an acid: it has no –COOH group to release H<sup>+</sup>. The two acidic ketone bodies are the ones that lower the pH.
Acetoacetate does release H<sup>+</sup>, but at blood pH it is an ion, and ions do not evaporate into the breath. The odor comes from the neutral, volatile ketone.
β-Hydroxybutyrate has a carboxylic acid group, so it does release H<sup>+</sup>. Its –OH and –COO<sup>−</sup> groups hold it in the blood, so it is not breathed out.

q: Starch digestion starts in the mouth but pauses while food is in the stomach. Why?
c: Stomach acid denatures salivary amylase, so the enzyme stops working
Pepsin in the stomach converts starch into amino acids instead
The starch has already been completely hydrolyzed to glucose in the mouth
The stomach has no water, and hydrolysis needs water
h: Amylase is a protein that works near neutral pH. What does a pH of 1–2 do to the shape of an enzyme?
w: Salivary amylase is swallowed with the food, but the low pH of the stomach denatures it. Starch digestion resumes in the small intestine, where the pH is raised again and pancreatic amylase takes over.
x: Pepsin hydrolyzes peptide bonds in proteins. It cannot act on the glycosidic bonds of starch, and starch contains no amino acids.
Food is in the mouth only briefly. Salivary amylase makes shorter chains (dextrins) and some maltose; most starch is digested in the small intestine.
Stomach contents are mostly water. The limit is the enzyme: no active amylase is present at that pH.

q: Stage I of catabolism (digestion) breaks each food into its building blocks. Which pairing is correct?
h: Think about which monomers each large food molecule was built from. Hydrolysis gives those monomers back.
w: Digestion is hydrolysis back to monomers: carbohydrates give monosaccharides, fats give fatty acids and glycerol, and proteins give amino acids.
x: Triacylglycerols are esters of glycerol and three fatty acids, so hydrolysis gives fatty acids and glycerol. Monosaccharides come from carbohydrates.
Starch is a polymer of glucose, so its hydrolysis gives glucose. Fatty acids and glycerol come from fats.
Acetyl CoA is made in Stage II, inside cells. Digestion stops at the building blocks, which for proteins are amino acids.

q: A bite of bread is swallowed and digested. In what order does its starch meet the carbohydrate-digesting enzymes?
c: salivary amylase (mouth) → pancreatic amylase (small intestine) → maltase (brush border)
maltase (mouth) → salivary amylase (stomach) → pancreatic amylase (small intestine)
pancreatic amylase (mouth) → salivary amylase (small intestine) → lactase (brush border)
h: Amylases shorten the long chain first. The enzyme that splits the disaccharide comes last, at the surface where the products are absorbed.
w: Salivary amylase begins breaking α(1→4) bonds in the mouth, pancreatic amylase finishes cutting the starch to maltose in the small intestine, and maltase on the brush border splits maltose into two glucose.
x: Maltase works last, on the brush border of the small intestine, and salivary amylase is inactive in the acid of the stomach.
Pepsin is a protein-digesting enzyme. Between the two ends of this list the starch needs pancreatic amylase.
The names give the sources: salivary amylase is in saliva and pancreatic amylase enters the small intestine. Lactase acts on lactose, not on the maltose made from starch.

q: How much ATP does the body capture when starch is hydrolyzed to glucose during digestion (Stage I)?
c: None; the small amount of energy released by hydrolysis is lost as heat
2 ATP per glucose, the same as glycolysis
10 ATP per glucose, the same as one acetyl CoA
None, because hydrolysis of starch needs ATP to be put in
h: Digestion only breaks glycosidic bonds with water. Where is the energy of the food after that step?
w: Digestion is hydrolysis by hydrolase enzymes. No ATP is made or spent in Stage I: the energy of the food is still stored in the glucose and is captured later, in Stages II and III.
x: The 2 ATP belong to glycolysis, a Stage II pathway that happens inside cells after glucose is absorbed.
10 ATP per acetyl CoA is the Stage III yield of the citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain. Nothing like that happens in the gut.
The answer 'none' is right, but the reason is wrong. Hydrolysis of a glycosidic bond releases a little energy and needs no ATP.

q: After sucrase, lactase and maltase finish their work, what happens to the glucose, fructose and galactose?
c: They are absorbed through the wall of the small intestine into the blood and go to the liver first
They are absorbed through the stomach wall and go directly to the muscles
They pass on to the large intestine and leave the body as fiber
They are joined into glycogen on the brush border before being absorbed
h: The three disaccharidases sit on the brush border. Where is that, and which organ receives the blood that leaves it?
w: The brush border enzymes release monosaccharides right where they are absorbed. They cross the wall of the small intestine into the blood (the portal vein) and reach the liver first, where fructose and galactose are converted into glycolysis intermediates.
x: Absorption of sugars happens in the small intestine, not the stomach, and the blood from the intestine goes to the liver before any other organ.
That is the fate of cellulose, which cannot be hydrolyzed. Free monosaccharides are absorbed.
Glycogen is built inside liver and muscle cells from glucose that has already been absorbed. Only monosaccharides cross the intestinal wall.

q: Activating one palmitic acid (16 carbons) to palmitoyl CoA costs the equivalent of 2 ATP. What does it cost to activate one stearic acid (18 carbons)?
c: 2 ATP, because activation is done once per fatty acid whatever its length
4 ATP, because a longer chain needs a second activation
9 ATP, one for each acetyl CoA that will be formed
16 ATP, two for each turn of β-oxidation
h: Activation attaches one coenzyme A to one –COOH group. How many –COOH groups does a fatty acid have, long or short?
w: A fatty acid has one carboxyl group, and activation joins it to one CoA using one ATP that is split to AMP. The cost is 2 ATP-equivalents per fatty acid, no matter how long the chain is.
