x: Chain length does not change the number of carboxyl groups. Only one CoA is attached, so only one activation is paid for.
Activation is not repeated for each two-carbon piece. The CoA for the later acetyl CoA units is added during β-oxidation without spending ATP.
The turns of β-oxidation produce FADH<sub>2</sub> and NADH; they do not use up ATP. The only ATP cost is the single activation step.

q: In fatty acid activation, R–COO<sup>−</sup> reacts with CoA–SH to give fatty acyl CoA, R–CO–S–CoA. Which functional group joins the fatty acid to coenzyme A?
h: Look at the atom between the C=O carbon and the CoA. Which element is it, and what is the oxygen version of this group called?
w: Coenzyme A ends in a thiol, –SH. Joining it to the acyl group gives C(=O)–S–, a thioester, which is an energy-rich form of the fatty acid ready for oxidation.
x: An ester has C(=O)–O–C. Here sulfur takes the place of that oxygen, which is what the prefix thio- means.
An amide has C(=O)–N. The fatty acid is bonded to the sulfur of CoA, not to a nitrogen.
A disulfide is an S–S bond, as between two cysteine side chains. Fatty acyl CoA has a single sulfur bonded to a carbonyl carbon.

q: Why does a long-chain fatty acyl CoA need the carnitine shuttle?
c: Fatty acyl CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane to reach the matrix
Carnitine supplies the ATP that is used to attach coenzyme A to the fatty acid
Carnitine carries fatty acids through the blood from fat cells to muscle
Carnitine oxidizes the fatty acid to acetyl CoA in the cytosol
h: Compare where the fatty acid is activated with where it will be oxidized. What lies between those two places?
w: Activation happens at the outer mitochondrial membrane, but β-oxidation happens in the matrix. Acyl CoA is too large to cross the inner membrane, so the acyl group is moved onto carnitine, carried across, and handed back to CoA inside.
x: Carnitine is a carrier, not an energy source. ATP itself (split to AMP) pays for attaching CoA, and that happens before the shuttle.
Transport in the blood is a different job, done by blood proteins and lipoproteins. Carnitine works at the mitochondrial membrane inside the cell.
Carnitine only carries the acyl group; it does not oxidize anything. β-Oxidation happens in the mitochondrial matrix, not the cytosol.

q: Where in the cell do fatty acid activation and β-oxidation take place?
c: Activation at the outer mitochondrial membrane; β-oxidation in the mitochondrial matrix
Activation in the mitochondrial matrix; β-oxidation at the outer mitochondrial membrane
Both in the mitochondrial matrix, so no transport is needed
Activation in the nucleus; β-oxidation in the mitochondrial matrix
h: The carnitine shuttle sits between these two steps. Which step has to come before the shuttle, and which after?
w: Acyl CoA synthetase on the outer mitochondrial membrane activates the fatty acid first. The carnitine shuttle then carries the acyl group through the inner membrane, and β-oxidation takes place in the matrix.
x: This reverses the two places. The fatty acid is activated outside, then carried in; oxidation is the inside step.
If both happened in the matrix there would be no need for carnitine. Long-chain fatty acids are activated before they cross the inner membrane.
The nucleus holds DNA and plays no part in fuel breakdown. Activation happens at the outer mitochondrial membrane.

q: Carnitine acyltransferase moves a fatty acyl group from coenzyme A onto carnitine. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: The enzyme's name tells you what it does. Is a group being moved from one molecule to another, joined with the help of ATP, split with water, or oxidized?
w: The acyl group is passed from one carrier (CoA) to another (carnitine) with no ATP, no water and no change in oxidation state. An enzyme that moves a group between molecules is a transferase.
x: A ligase joins two molecules using the energy of ATP. That describes acyl CoA synthetase in the activation step, not the shuttle enzyme.
A hydrolase breaks a bond with water. Here the acyl group goes to carnitine, not to water, so no free fatty acid is released.
An oxidoreductase needs a coenzyme such as NAD<sup>+</sup> or FAD and changes the oxidation state. Oxidation of the fatty acid starts later, in β-oxidation.

q: Why does the body convert the nitrogen from amino acids into urea instead of letting ammonia build up?
c: Ammonia is a toxic base, while urea is neutral, relatively nontoxic and very soluble in water
Urea is insoluble in water, so it is easy to store in the liver
Making urea from ammonia produces ATP for the liver
Ammonia cannot dissolve in blood, so it could never reach the kidneys
h: Compare the two molecules as waste products: which one is harmful to cells, and which one can be carried safely in the blood and excreted in urine?
w: Ammonia (and NH4+) is extremely toxic, especially to the brain. The urea cycle turns it into urea, a small, neutral, water-soluble and relatively nontoxic molecule that the blood carries to the kidneys.
x: Urea is very soluble in water, which is exactly why it can travel in the blood and leave in urine. It is not stored.
The urea cycle uses energy: the equivalent of 3 ATP is spent for each urea. The body pays this to get rid of a poison.
Ammonia dissolves readily in water as NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>. The problem is its toxicity, not its solubility.

q: In a liver cell, where do the reactions of the urea cycle take place?
c: The entry step and step 1 in the mitochondrial matrix; steps 2–4 in the cytosol
Every step is in the mitochondrial matrix
Every step is in the cytosol
The entry step and step 1 in the cytosol; steps 2–4 in the mitochondrial matrix
h: Citrulline is made in one compartment and then transported to another. Where is carbamoyl phosphate made?
w: Carbamoyl phosphate is made in the mitochondrial matrix and added to ornithine there to give citrulline. Citrulline then moves to the cytosol for steps 2–4, and ornithine returns to the mitochondrion.
x: The citric acid cycle and β-oxidation are entirely in the matrix, but the urea cycle is split between two compartments.
Glycolysis is entirely in the cytosol, but the urea cycle begins inside the mitochondrion, where carbamoyl phosphate is made.
This reverses the compartments. The cycle starts in the matrix, and urea is released in the cytosol by arginase.

q: Urea, H<sub>2</sub>N–CO–NH<sub>2</sub>, has one carbon atom. Where does that carbon come from?
c: the acetyl group of acetyl CoA
h: Look at what is combined with NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> in the entry step to make carbamoyl phosphate.
w: In the entry step NH4+ and HCO3− are joined, using 2 ATP, to make carbamoyl phosphate. The C=O of urea is that bicarbonate carbon, so the cycle disposes of CO2 as well as nitrogen.
x: Aspartate gives only its amino nitrogen. Its four carbons leave the cycle as fumarate.
Ornithine is a carrier that is regenerated unchanged at the end of every turn, so none of its atoms end up in urea.
Acetyl CoA is the fuel of the citric acid cycle. It does not enter the urea cycle.

q: Making one urea costs the equivalent of 3 ATP. Where is that ATP spent?
c: 2 ATP to make carbamoyl phosphate (entry step) and 1 ATP when citrulline joins aspartate (step 2)
1 ATP in each of the last three steps of the cycle
3 ATP in the final step, when arginine is hydrolyzed to urea and ornithine
1 ATP to make carbamoyl phosphate and 2 ATP to split argininosuccinate
h: ATP is needed where two molecules are joined (ligase steps). Which two steps of the cycle bring in a nitrogen atom?
w: Both nitrogen-adding steps are ligase reactions that need ATP: 2 ATP at the entry step (NH4+ + HCO3− → carbamoyl phosphate) and 1 ATP, split to AMP, at step 2 (citrulline + aspartate).
x: Steps 3 and 4 use no ATP. Step 3 is a cleavage by a lyase and step 4 is a hydrolysis.
The arginase step is a hydrolysis; water does the splitting and no ATP is used.
The numbers are placed on the wrong steps. Carbamoyl phosphate takes 2 ATP, and splitting argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate takes none.

q: Patient A has a high blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and normal blood ammonia. Patient B has a normal BUN and high blood ammonia. What do these results mean chemically?
c: A: urea is being made but not excreted. B: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is not being converted to urea
A: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is not being converted to urea. B: urea is being made but not excreted
A and B: urea is being made but not excreted
A: urea is being broken back down to NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>. B: too much urea is being made
h: Follow the nitrogen: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> → urea in the liver, then urea → urine through the kidneys. Which substance piles up when each step is blocked?
w: Whatever sits just before a blocked step accumulates. High urea with normal ammonia means the urea cycle works but urea is not being removed (kidneys); high ammonia with normal urea means the urea cycle itself is failing (liver).
x: This reverses the two. If NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> were not being converted, ammonia would be high, which is Patient B's result.
The two patients have different substances elevated, so the blocked step cannot be the same. Patient B's urea level is normal.
Neither result fits. Breaking urea down would raise ammonia in Patient A, and making too much urea would raise BUN in Patient B.
